Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/stack-basics.html

Pattern: Queue (FIFO) — If you see: "level by level", "shortest path in an unweighted graph", "nearest", "process in arrival order", "recent requests in a time window" → think: ArrayDeque with offer/poll; BFS. Time O(V + E).

BFS preview

grid BFS from S, 4 directions; numbers = distance (level)
  S 1 2          q after each level:
  1 # 3          level 0: [S]
  2 3 4          level 1: [(0,1) (1,0)]
                 level 2: [(0,2) (2,0)]
                 level 3: [(1,2) (2,1)]
                 level 4: [(2,2)]
Deque<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
boolean[][] seen = new boolean[m][n];
q.offer(new int[]{sr, sc});
seen[sr][sc] = true;  // mark when ENQUEUED, not when polled
for (int dist = 0; !q.isEmpty(); dist++) {
    for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {      // one full level
        int[] cell = q.poll();
        // process cell at distance dist; for each valid neighbour not seen:
        //   seen[nr][nc] = true; q.offer(new int[]{nr, nc});
    }
}

Full BFS patterns (multi-source, 0-1 BFS, topological sort) are in the graphs chapter.

Trap: Marking seen when you poll instead of when you offer lets the same cell be enqueued many times — correct answer, exponential blow-up on grids.

Number of Recent Calls (LC 933)

Key insight: timestamps arrive increasing; the queue holds the window [t - 3000, t]. Drop from the front while too old.

Step by step

  1. Add the new timestamp t to the back of the queue.
  2. While the front is older than t - 3000, remove it from the front.
  3. The queue now holds exactly the calls in the window; return its size.
class RecentCounter {
    private final Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    public int ping(int t) {
        q.offer(t);
        while (q.peek() < t - 3000) q.poll();
        return q.size();
    }
}

Amortized O(1).

Implement Queue using Stacks (LC 232)

Key insight: two stacks — in receives pushes; out serves pops. Only when out is empty, pour all of in into out, which reverses the order once. Each element moves at most once: amortized O(1).

push 1, push 2, push 3     in: [1 2 3>   out: [ >          (> marks the top)
pop  -> out empty, pour    in: [ >       out: [3 2 1>  -> pop 1
push 4                     in: [4>       out: [3 2>
pop  -> out not empty      -> pop 2      (4 waits in "in" until out is empty)
pop  -> 3
pop  -> out empty, pour 4 -> pop 4
class MyQueue {
    private final Deque<Integer> in = new ArrayDeque<>(), out = new ArrayDeque<>();
    public void push(int x) { in.push(x); }
    public int pop()        { peek(); return out.pop(); }
    public int peek() {
        if (out.isEmpty()) while (!in.isEmpty()) out.push(in.pop());  // pour only when em
        return out.peek();
    }
    public boolean empty()  { return in.isEmpty() && out.isEmpty(); }
}

Amortized O(1) per operation, worst case O(n) for one pop. The reverse (LC 225, stack using one queue): after each push, rotate the queue size - 1 times so the new element is at the front — push O(n), pop O(1).

Trap: Pouring in into out while out still has elements breaks FIFO order. Pour only when out is empty.

6.15 Monotonic deque: Sliding Window Maximum (LC 239)

In plain words: For the maximum of each window of size 3, keep indices in a deque whose values fall from front to back. A new number throws out smaller numbers from the back (they can never be the max again); an index that left the window drops off the front. The front is the window maximum.

Analogy: a queue of job applicants where a stronger, younger applicant makes weaker, older ones give up; the front is the best still eligible.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/monotonic-stack.html

Pattern: Monotonic deque — If you see: "maximum/minimum of every window of size k", "shortest subarray with sum at least K" (with negatives), "constrained subsequence sum" → think: deque of indices with decreasing values; drop expired indices from the front, drop smaller values from the back; front is the window max. Time O(n), space O(k).

Say this aloud: "An element that is smaller than a newer element can never be a window max again, because the newer one outlives it. So I throw it away from the back. The front is always the max of the current window; I drop it when it slides out."

nums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3
deque shows index(value), front -> back; window = [i-k+1, i]

i  val  expire front?   pop smaller from back    deque after push       max
0   1   -               -                        0(1)
1   3   -               pop 0(1)                 1(3)
2  -1   -               -                        1(3) 2(-1)             3
3  -3   front 1 >= 1 ok -                        1(3) 2(-1) 3(-3)       3
4   5   front 1 < 2 out pop 3(-3), 2(-1)         4(5)                   5
5   3   -               -                        4(5) 5(3)              5
6   6   front 4 >= 4 ok pop 5(3), 4(5)           6(6)                   6
7   7   -               pop 6(6)                 7(7)                   7
result [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]
public int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] nums, int k) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] res = new int[n - k + 1];
    Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();                  // indices, values decreasing
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) dq.pollFirst();   // expired
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && nums[dq.peekLast()] <= nums[i]) dq.pollLast();
        dq.offerLast(i);
        if (i >= k - 1) res[i - k + 1] = nums[dq.peekFirst()];
    }
    return res;
}

O(n): every index enters and leaves the deque once.

Structure Window max per step Total
Recompute each window O(k) O(nk)
Max-heap with lazy deletion O(log n) O(n log n)
TreeMap counts O(log k) O(n log k)
Monotonic deque O(1) amortized O(n)

Remember: Monotonic deque = monotonic stack with an exit at the front for expired indices. Back: pop the weaker. Front: pop the expired. Front = answer.

Trap: Storing values instead of indices — you then cannot tell when the front has left the window.

6.16 Design Circular Queue (LC 622)

In plain words: Use a fixed array of size k, a head index and a size count. The back is (head + size) % k, so when the end of the array is reached, positions wrap around to index 0. With k = 4, after 4 adds it is full; one remove frees slot head.

Analogy: a round table with numbered seats: after the last seat, the next guest sits in seat 0 again.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/stack-basics.html

Key insight: fixed array, a head index and a size. The tail position is computed: (head + size) % cap. Using size avoids the classic "is it full or empty when head == tail?" ambiguity.

capacity 4
enQueue 1,2,3:   [1 2 3 _]   head=0 size=3   rear index = (0+3-1)%4 = 2
deQueue:         [_ 2 3 _]   head=1 size=2
enQueue 4,5:     [5 2 3 4]   head=1 size=4   5 went to (1+3)%4 = 0 (wrapped)
isFull -> true;  Front = a[1] = 2;  Rear = a[(1+4-1)%4] = a[0] = 5
class MyCircularQueue {
    private final int[] a;
    private int head = 0, size = 0;

    public MyCircularQueue(int k) { a = new int[k]; }

    public boolean enQueue(int value) {
        if (isFull()) return false;
        a[(head + size) % a.length] = value;
        size++;
        return true;
    }
    public boolean deQueue() {
        if (isEmpty()) return false;
        head = (head + 1) % a.length;
        size--;
        return true;
    }
    public int Front()  { return isEmpty() ? -1 : a[head]; }
    public int Rear()   { return isEmpty() ? -1 : a[(head + size - 1) % a.length]; }
    public boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; }
    public boolean isFull()  { return size == a.length; }
}

All O(1). This is exactly how ArrayDeque works internally (with a power-of-two capacity and & (cap - 1) instead of %, and doubling when full).

Tip: In a system-design follow-up, a circular buffer is the answer for "keep the last N log lines / metrics in fixed memory" and for producer-consumer ring buffers (LMAX Disruptor).

6.17 Which structure? (decision picture)

In plain words: Ask what order you need things back in. Newest first → stack. Oldest first → queue. Nearest bigger or smaller → monotonic stack. Max or min of a moving window → monotonic deque.

Analogy: choosing a container in a kitchen: a plate pile, a ticket line, or a sorted spice rack — each makes one kind of "next" easy.

6.z Chapter cheat sheet

Trigger Pattern Template one-liner Complexity
brackets, balanced, nested Matching stack push expected closer; pop must equal O(n)
O(1) min with push/pop Stack of {val, min} min = Math.min(val, peek()[1]) O(1)
postfix expression Operand stack b = pop(); a = pop(); push(a op b) O(n)
all valid bracket strings Backtracking add ( if open < n, ) if close < open O(Catalan)
+ - * / string Running res + last apply previous op when next op arrives O(n)
parentheses with + - Push (res, sign) on ): res = res * pop() + pop() O(n)
k[...] encoding Two stacks (counts, strings) on ]: outer + cur.repeat(k) O(output)
unix path Deque as stack .. pops, ./empty skip O(n)
collisions, cancel out Stack with while-loop pop while top loses O(n)
next greater / days until warmer Decreasing stack pop while a[i] > a[top], res[j] = i - j O(n)
circular next greater Loop 2n, i % n push only when i < n O(n)
span / previous greater Stack of (price, span) absorb popped spans O(1) amortized
largest rectangle Increasing stack + sentinel 0 h * (i - newTop - 1) O(n)
smallest number after k removals Increasing stack + budget pop while top > c and k > 0 O(n)

Never forget

  • ArrayDeque for stacks and queues; never Stack. push/pop/peek = stack, offer/poll/peek = queue.
  • Push the expected closer in bracket matching; end with isEmpty().
  • RPN: the first pop is the right operand.
  • Basic Calculator II: res + last; apply the previous operator when a new one (or the end) arrives.
  • Monotonic stack stores indices, not values.
  • Next greater → decreasing stack. Next smaller → increasing stack.
  • The popped element's answer is the current index; the previous-element answer is the new top.
  • Each index is pushed once and popped once → O(n), despite the nested while.
  • Histogram: sentinel 0 at the end; width = i - newTop - 1.
  • Duplicates in contribution problems: one side strict, other side non-strict.
  • Circular arrays: iterate 2n with i % n, push only in the first pass.
  • Remove K Digits: cut leftover k from the end, strip leading zeros, empty → "0".
  • Sliding window max: deque of indices, decreasing values; expire front, pop weaker back.
  • BFS: mark seen when enqueuing.
  • Queue from stacks: pour in into out only when out is empty — amortized O(1).

7. Trees and Binary Search Trees

Trees are the single most common topic in coding rounds after arrays. The good news: almost every tree problem is the same recursive function with a different body. Learn the three questions in 7.2 and you can write most of these solutions without having seen them before.

7.1 The node, the words, the shapes

In plain words: A tree is boxes joined by arrows that only point down. The top box is the root; a box with no children is a leaf. In a binary tree every box has at most 2 children, left and right. A tree of 7 boxes in 3 full levels has height 3; the root is at depth 0.

Analogy: A family tree drawn upside down: one ancestor at the top, children below, and the people with no children at the bottom are the leaves.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/tree-traversals.html

Say this aloud first: "A binary tree is a node with a value and at most two children; every subtree is itself a binary tree, so recursion fits naturally."

public class TreeNode {
    int val;
    TreeNode left, right;
    TreeNode() {}
    TreeNode(int val) { this.val = val; }
    TreeNode(int val, TreeNode left, TreeNode right) {
        this.val = val; this.left = left; this.right = right;
    }
}

Vocabulary picture

                 depth 0      height of tree = 3 (edges on longest root->leaf path)
        [1]  <-- root
       /   \
     [2]   [3]       depth 1  (depth = edges from ROOT down to the node)
    /  \      \
  [4]  [5]    [6]    depth 2
       /
     [7]  <-- leaf   depth 3  (leaf = no children)

  height(node) = edges on longest path DOWN to a leaf  h(7)=0, h(5)=1, h(1)=3
  depth(node)  = edges on path UP to the root            depth(7)=3
  Height is measured from below, depth from above.

Many LeetCode problems count nodes instead of edges ("maximum depth = number of nodes on the longest path"). Always confirm which one the problem means; the code differs by one.

Tree shapes

  FULL: every node has 0 or 2 children    COMPLETE: all levels full except last,
                                          last filled LEFT to RIGHT (heaps!)
        o                                       o
       / \                                    /   \
      o   o                                  o     o
         / \                                / \   /
        o   o                              o   o o

  PERFECT: full AND all leaves same depth   BALANCED: |h(left) - h(right)| <= 1
                                            at EVERY node -> height O(log n)
        o                                       o
      /   \                                    / \
     o     o                                  o   o
    / \   / \                                /
   o   o o   o      nodes = 2^(h+1) - 1     o

  DEGENERATE (a linked list): height n-1, every op O(n)
   o
    \
     o
      \
       o
Term One-liner
Full 0 or 2 children everywhere
Complete Filled level by level, left to right; stored in an array (heap)
Perfect Full and all leaves on the same level; 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes
Balanced Left and right heights differ by at most 1 at every node
BST left subtree < node < right subtree, at every node

Tip: Recursion depth on a tree equals its height. Balanced: O(log n) stack. Skewed: O(n) stack, and 10^5 nodes in a line can overflow Java's default stack. Mention this and offer an iterative version when the input can be a line.

7.2 The 3 questions that solve any tree problem

In plain words: Stand on one node and ignore the rest of the tree. Ask: what do I need from my two children, what do I hand back to my parent, and what does my parent hand to me? For max depth: I need both children's depths (say 2 and 3) and I return 1 + 3 = 4.

Analogy: A manager who only talks to two direct reports: ask each "how deep is your team?", take the bigger answer, add 1 for yourself, and report it upwards.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/tree-recursion.html

Say: "I'll write a recursive function and decide what each call needs from its children, what it returns to its parent, and what it receives from its parent."

Pattern: Tree recursion — If you see: binary tree, "for every node", path, depth, subtree → think: answer the 3 questions, then write dfs(node). Time O(n), space O(h).

                 +---------------------------------+
   Q3 PASS DOWN  |  what does a node need to know  |   (depth so far, path sum so far,
   ------------> |  from ABOVE?  -> parameter      |    max seen on path, min/max bounds)
                 +---------------------------------+
                         |                 |
                    dfs(left)          dfs(right)
                         |                 |
                 +---------------------------------+
   Q1 NEED       |  what do I need from my         |   (height of each side, is it
   <------------ |  children? -> recursive results |    balanced, best path down)
                 +---------------------------------+
   Q2 RETURN UP  |  what single value does my      |   (my height, my best one-sided
                 |  parent need? -> return value   |    path, -1 for "invalid")
                 +---------------------------------+
Problem Q1: need from children Q2: return up Q3: pass down
Max depth their depths 1 + max nothing
Path sum did a child find it boolean remaining sum
Good nodes their counts count max on path so far
Validate BST are they valid boolean (min, max) bounds
Diameter their heights my height nothing (global answer)
Balanced their heights or -1 height or -1 nothing

Top-down vs bottom-up

  TOP-DOWN (preorder flavour)              BOTTOM-UP (postorder flavour)
  state flows DOWN as parameters           values flow UP as return values

        [1]  depth=1                            [1]  return 1+max(2,1)=3
       /   \                                   /   \
     [2]   [3] depth=2                       [2]   [3] return 1
     /                                       /
   [4] depth=3 -> update global max        [4] return 1 (null children return 0)

  "Tell the child what it needs."          "Ask the children, then combine."
  Use when: running path state             Use when: answer for a node depends on
  (sum so far, max so far, bounds)         its subtrees (height, size, balanced)
// TOP-DOWN template: carry state in parameters, record answer at the right node
int best = 0;
void topDown(TreeNode node, int depth) {
    if (node == null) return;
    if (node.left == null && node.right == null) best = Math.max(best, depth); // leaf
    topDown(node.left, depth + 1);
    topDown(node.right, depth + 1);
}

// BOTTOM-UP template: combine children's results, return one value
int bottomUp(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;          // base case: value for empty tree
    int l = bottomUp(node.left);         // Q1
    int r = bottomUp(node.right);
    return 1 + Math.max(l, r);           // Q2
}

Remember: Parameters go DOWN, return values come UP. If the answer at a node depends on its subtrees, it is bottom-up.

Trap: Forgetting the null base case, or using a leaf check where a null check is needed (a node with one child is not a leaf). Decide: "what does an empty tree return?" before writing anything else.

7.3 Traversals: DFS three ways and BFS

In plain words: Every walk visits all n nodes once; the orders differ only in when you write a node down. Pre-order writes me first, in-order writes me between my children, post-order writes me last. BFS writes floor by floor using a queue: for root 1 with children 2 and 3, BFS gives 1, 2, 3.

Analogy: Reading a company chart: the boss first (pre-order), the boss after the whole left team (in-order), the boss only after both teams reported (post-order), or one floor at a time (BFS).

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/tree-traversals.html

Pattern: Traversal — If you see: "print / collect nodes in order", "level by level", "copy", "serialize" → think: pre/in/post-order DFS or BFS with a queue. Time O(n), space O(h) for DFS, O(width) for BFS.

  Example tree used below:         Order          Rule                   Output
           1                       Pre-order      Node, Left, Right      1 2 4 5 3
          / \                      In-order       Left, Node, Right      4 2 5 1 3
         2   3                     Post-order     Left, Right, Node      4 5 2 3 1
        / \                        Level-order    row by row             1 2 3 4 5
       4   5
  Mnemonic: the name says where the NODE goes: PRE = first, IN = middle, POST = last.

Recursive DFS (all three in one place)

void dfs(TreeNode node, List<Integer> res) {
    if (node == null) return;
    // res.add(node.val);   PRE-order here
    dfs(node.left, res);
    // res.add(node.val);   IN-order here
    dfs(node.right, res);
    // res.add(node.val);   POST-order here
}

Iterative pre-order (stack, push right first)

List<Integer> preorder(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return res;
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    stack.push(root);
    while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
        TreeNode node = stack.pop();
        res.add(node.val);
        if (node.right != null) stack.push(node.right); // right first...
        if (node.left != null) stack.push(node.left);   // ...so left pops first
    }
    return res;
}
  Trace on tree 1(2(4,5),3)          stack (top on the right)    res
  start                              [1]                         []
  pop 1, push 3, push 2              [3, 2]                      [1]
  pop 2, push 5, push 4              [3, 5, 4]                   [1, 2]
  pop 4                              [3, 5]                      [1, 2, 4]
  pop 5                              [3]                         [1, 2, 4, 5]
  pop 3                              []                          [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]

Iterative in-order (go left as far as possible)

This is the most important iterative traversal: BST iterator, Kth smallest and Validate BST all reuse it.

List<Integer> inorder(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
        while (cur != null) {          // 1. dive left, stacking the path
            stack.push(cur);
            cur = cur.left;
        }
        cur = stack.pop();             // 2. leftmost unvisited node
        res.add(cur.val);              // 3. visit
        cur = cur.right;               // 4. then its right subtree
    }
    return res;
}
  Trace on tree 1(2(4,5),3)
  step              cur     stack (top right)    res
  dive left         null    [1, 2, 4]            []
  pop 4, go right   null    [1, 2]               [4]
  pop 2, go right   5       [1]                  [4, 2]
  dive left         null    [1, 5]               [4, 2]
  pop 5, go right   null    [1]                  [4, 2, 5]
  pop 1, go right   3       []                   [4, 2, 5, 1]
  dive left         null    [3]                  [4, 2, 5, 1]
  pop 3, go right   null    []                   [4, 2, 5, 1, 3]   loop ends

Iterative post-order (reverse of a modified pre-order)

Post-order is Left, Right, Node. Reverse it: Node, Right, Left, which is pre-order with the push order swapped. Collect that, then reverse.

List<Integer> postorder(TreeNode root) {
    LinkedList<Integer> res = new LinkedList<>();
    if (root == null) return res;
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    stack.push(root);
    while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
        TreeNode node = stack.pop();
        res.addFirst(node.val);                          // prepend = reverse for free
        if (node.left != null) stack.push(node.left);    // left first...
        if (node.right != null) stack.push(node.right);  // ...so right pops first
    }
    return res;
}
  pops in order: 1, 3, 2, 5, 4    (Node, Right, Left)
  addFirst each:  [1] -> [3,1] -> [2,3,1] -> [5,2,3,1] -> [4,5,2,3,1]   = post-order

BFS level order (queue, freeze the level size)

List<List<Integer>> levelOrder(TreeNode root) {
    List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return res;
    Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.offer(root);
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int size = q.size();                 // freeze: nodes of THIS level only
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            TreeNode node = q.poll();
            level.add(node.val);
            if (node.left != null) q.offer(node.left);
            if (node.right != null) q.offer(node.right);
        }
        res.add(level);
    }
    return res;
}
  Trace on tree 1(2(4,5),3)          queue (front on the left)    res
  start                              [1]                          []
  level size 1: poll 1, add 2,3      [2, 3]                       [[1]]
  level size 2: poll 2 add 4,5;      [4, 5]                       [[1],[2,3]]
                poll 3
  level size 2: poll 4, poll 5       []                           [[1],[2,3],[4,5]]

Remember: Stack = DFS, queue = BFS. In-order iterative = "dive left, pop, go right". Level order = "freeze q.size() before the for loop".

Trap: Reading q.size() inside the for-loop condition. The queue grows while you add children, so the level boundary is lost. Store it in size first.

Tip: ArrayDeque does not accept null. Check children for null before offer/push, or you get a NullPointerException.

7.4 Warm-up recursion problems

In plain words: Each problem here is two or three lines: handle the empty tree, call yourself on the left and right child, and combine the two answers. Depth of a leaf is 1 + max(0, 0) = 1; its parent is 1 + 1 = 2, and so on upwards.

Analogy: Russian dolls: you only open one doll, trust that the smaller dolls inside are handled the same way, and close it again.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/tree-recursion.html

Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (LC 104)

Key insight: depth = 1 + deeper child; empty tree has depth 0.

Step by step:

  1. If the node is null, its depth is 0.
  2. Ask the left child for its depth and the right child for its depth.
  3. Return 1 (this node) + the larger of the two.
int maxDepth(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return 0;
    return 1 + Math.max(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right));
}

O(n) time, O(h) space. Iterative alternative: BFS and count levels.

Same Tree (LC 100)

Key insight: two trees are equal if roots match and both subtree pairs are equal.

boolean isSameTree(TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (p == null && q == null) return true;
    if (p == null || q == null || p.val != q.val) return false;
    return isSameTree(p.left, q.left) && isSameTree(p.right, q.right);
}

O(n) time, O(h) space.

Invert Binary Tree (LC 226)

Key insight: swap the children at every node, in any order.

        4                    4
       / \                  / \
      2   7       ->       7   2
     / \ / \              / \ / \
    1  3 6  9            9  6 3  1
TreeNode invertTree(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return null;
    TreeNode tmp = root.left;
    root.left = invertTree(root.right);
    root.right = invertTree(tmp);
    return root;
}

O(n) time, O(h) space.

Symmetric Tree (LC 101)

Key insight: compare the tree with its mirror; walk two pointers outward (left.left with right.right) and inward (left.right with right.left).

         1
       /   \
      2  =  2          outer pair: 3 vs 3
     / \   / \         inner pair: 4 vs 4
    3   4 4   3
boolean isSymmetric(TreeNode root) {
    return mirror(root.left, root.right);
}
boolean mirror(TreeNode a, TreeNode b) {
    if (a == null && b == null) return true;
    if (a == null || b == null || a.val != b.val) return false;
    return mirror(a.left, b.right) && mirror(a.right, b.left);
}

O(n) time, O(h) space.

Subtree of Another Tree (LC 572)

Key insight: at every node of root, ask "is the tree starting here the same as subRoot?" — reuse Same Tree.

boolean isSubtree(TreeNode root, TreeNode subRoot) {
    if (root == null) return false;
    if (isSameTree(root, subRoot)) return true;
    return isSubtree(root.left, subRoot) || isSubtree(root.right, subRoot);
}

O(m·n) worst case. Follow-up answer: serialize both trees with null markers ("#") and use KMP for O(m + n).

Trap: Serializing without null markers breaks Subtree: 2(1, null) and 2(null, 1) both print 2 1. Always mark nulls and wrap values (",2,1,#,#,#") so 12 does not match 2.

Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree (LC 1448)

Key insight: top-down — pass the max seen on the path; a node is good if val >= max.

          3            path max passed down
         / \
       (1)  4          1 < 3 -> not good;  4 >= 3 -> good
       /   / \
      3   1   5        3 >= 3 good; 1 < 4 not; 5 >= 4 good     answer = 4
int goodNodes(TreeNode root) { return count(root, Integer.MIN_VALUE); }
int count(TreeNode node, int max) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int good = node.val >= max ? 1 : 0;
    int m = Math.max(max, node.val);
    return good + count(node.left, m) + count(node.right, m);
}

O(n) time, O(h) space. Top-down state, bottom-up count: both directions in one function.

7.5 The "global answer, return something else" trick

In plain words: The longest path can bend at a node: down the left side and down the right side. The parent cannot use a bent path, only one straight branch. So each node returns its height (say 3) but writes left + right (say 2 + 2 = 4) into a global best.

Analogy: Asking each manager for the longest chain below them (what the boss can extend) while secretly noting the longest chain that passes through each manager.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/tree-recursion.html

Pattern: Global answer + different return — If you see: "longest path between any two nodes", "max path sum anywhere", "check a property at every node" → think: the return value is the one-sided thing the parent can extend; the answer is updated in a field. Time O(n), space O(h).

The key fact: a path that bends at a node can use both children, but a parent can only extend one branch. So the function returns the best one-sided value, and the two-sided value goes into a global.

            [P]  parent can only continue ONE arm, so return max(L, R) + me
             |
            [N]  <-- the path may BEND here: L + me + R  -> update global answer
           /   \
         L-arm  R-arm

Diameter of Binary Tree (LC 543)

Key insight: diameter through a node = height(left) + height(right) in edges; return height, track max sum.

Step by step:

  1. Keep a field best = 0.
  2. At each node get the height of the left and right subtrees (null = 0).
  3. left + right is the longest path bending here: update best.
  4. Return 1 + max(left, right) so the parent can extend one branch.
          1               at node 2: left h=1 (via 4), right h=1 (via 5) -> 2 edges
         / \              at node 1: left h=2 (via 2), right h=1 (via 3) -> 3 edges
        2   3             answer = 3   (path 4-2-1-3)
       / \
      4   5
int diameter = 0;
int diameterOfBinaryTree(TreeNode root) {
    height(root);
    return diameter;
}
int height(TreeNode node) {            // returns height in NODES on the longest arm
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int l = height(node.left), r = height(node.right);
    diameter = Math.max(diameter, l + r);   // edges through node = l + r
    return 1 + Math.max(l, r);
}

O(n) time, O(h) space.

Balanced Binary Tree (LC 110)

Key insight: return height, or -1 as a sentinel meaning "unbalanced below"; short-circuit once you see -1. One pass, O(n).

boolean isBalanced(TreeNode root) { return check(root) != -1; }
int check(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int l = check(node.left);
    if (l == -1) return -1;
    int r = check(node.right);
    if (r == -1) return -1;
    if (Math.abs(l - r) > 1) return -1;
    return 1 + Math.max(l, r);
}

Trap: The naive version calls height() at every node from the top: O(n^2) on a skewed tree. Interviewers ask for the O(n) -1 sentinel version.

Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (LC 124)

Key insight: return the best one-sided sum going down (never below 0, drop negative arms); update the global with left + node + right.

        -10                  gain(9)  = 9
        /  \                 gain(15) = 15, gain(7) = 7
       9    20               at 20: path = 15 + 20 + 7 = 42  -> best = 42
           /  \                     return 20 + max(15,7) = 35
          15   7             at -10: path = 9 + (-10) + 35 = 34 < 42
                             answer = 42
int best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
int maxPathSum(TreeNode root) {
    gain(root);
    return best;
}
int gain(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int l = Math.max(0, gain(node.left));    // negative arm? don't take it
    int r = Math.max(0, gain(node.right));
    best = Math.max(best, l + node.val + r); // path bending here
    return node.val + Math.max(l, r);        // one arm for the parent
}

O(n) time, O(h) space.

Trap: Initialise best to Integer.MIN_VALUE, not 0. With an all-negative tree like [-3] the answer is -3.

Remember: "Bend here, return one arm." Global gets both arms, parent gets one.

7.6 Path sum family

In plain words: Carry "how much is still needed" down the tree. Target 22, root 5: the children are told 17. Every node subtracts its own value; at a leaf, the answer is yes only if the amount left is exactly 0.

Analogy: Paying tolls on a road trip with a fixed budget: each town takes its toll, and you succeed only if you reach a dead end with exactly zero money left.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/tree-recursion.html

Pattern: Root-to-leaf / any-path sums — If you see: "path sum", "sum equals target", "count paths" → think: pass remaining sum down (I, II); prefix-sum hash map on the root-to-node path (III). Time O(n), space O(h).

Path Sum (LC 112)

Key insight: subtract as you go down; at a leaf, check whether the remainder is zero.

Step by step:

  1. A null node returns false.
  2. Subtract the node's value from the target.
  3. At a leaf, return whether the target left is exactly 0.
  4. Otherwise return left result OR right result, passing the new target down.
boolean hasPathSum(TreeNode root, int target) {
    if (root == null) return false;
    target -= root.val;
    if (root.left == null && root.right == null) return target == 0;
    return hasPathSum(root.left, target) || hasPathSum(root.right, target);
}

Path Sum II (LC 113)

Key insight: backtracking — add the node to the path, recurse, remove it.

List<List<Integer>> pathSum(TreeNode root, int target) {
    List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
    walk(root, target, new ArrayList<>(), res);
    return res;
}
void walk(TreeNode node, int rem, List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> res) {
    if (node == null) return;
    path.add(node.val);
    rem -= node.val;
    boolean leaf = node.left == null && node.right == null;
    if (leaf && rem == 0) res.add(new ArrayList<>(path));
    walk(node.left, rem, path, res);
    walk(node.right, rem, path, res);
    path.remove(path.size() - 1);             // backtrack
}

O(n^2) worst case because of copying paths; O(h) extra space.

Trap: res.add(path) adds the same list object that you keep mutating. Copy it: new ArrayList<>(path).

Path Sum III (LC 437) — prefix sum on a tree

Key insight: same as "subarray sum equals K" (chapter on hashing), applied to the single root-to-node path. A downward path ending here has sum target iff some ancestor prefix equals cur - target. Remove the prefix when you return (backtrack), because siblings are not on the same path.

  target = 8          path from root to node 3 (bottom):  10 -> 5 -> 3
        10            prefix sums on this path: 0 (empty), 10, 15, 18
       /              at node 3: cur = 18, need 18 - 8 = 10 -> prefix 10 exists once
      5                         -> path [5, 3] sums to 8, count += 1
     /
    3                 map = {0:1, 10:1, 15:1, 18:1}   (0 is the "start at root" case)
int pathSum(TreeNode root, int target) {
    Map<Long, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
    seen.put(0L, 1);
    return count(root, 0L, target, seen);
}
int count(TreeNode node, long cur, int target, Map<Long, Integer> seen) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    cur += node.val;
    int res = seen.getOrDefault(cur - target, 0);
    seen.merge(cur, 1, Integer::sum);
    res += count(node.left, cur, target, seen) + count(node.right, cur, target, seen);
    seen.merge(cur, -1, Integer::sum);       // backtrack: leave this path
    return res;
}

O(n) time, O(h) space. Use long: LeetCode includes sums that overflow int.

Remember: "Subarray sum = k" on a tree = prefix map + remove on the way back up.

7.7 BFS level problems

In plain words: Put the root in a queue. For each floor, first read size = queue size (say 3), then take exactly 3 nodes out and add their children at the back. Those children are the next floor. Right side view = the last node of each floor.

Analogy: Evacuating a building floor by floor: count the people on this floor, send exactly that many out, and the people they call down form the next group.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/tree-bfs.html

Pattern: Level order — If you see: "level", "row", "right side", "zigzag", "width", "minimum depth", "nearest" → think: BFS with size = q.size() per level. Time O(n), space O(width).

Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (LC 102)

The template in 7.3 is the full solution.

Zigzag Level Order (LC 103)

Key insight: normal BFS; add to the front of the level list on odd levels.

       3              level 0 L->R: [3]
      / \             level 1 R->L: [20, 9]
     9   20           level 2 L->R: [15, 7]
        /  \
       15   7
List<List<Integer>> zigzagLevelOrder(TreeNode root) {
    List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return res;
    Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.offer(root);
    boolean leftToRight = true;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int size = q.size();
        LinkedList<Integer> level = new LinkedList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            TreeNode node = q.poll();
            if (leftToRight) level.addLast(node.val); else level.addFirst(node.val);
            if (node.left != null) q.offer(node.left);
            if (node.right != null) q.offer(node.right);
        }
        res.add(level);
        leftToRight = !leftToRight;
    }
    return res;
}

Binary Tree Right Side View (LC 199)

Key insight: the last node polled in each level is visible from the right.

        1   <- see 1
       / \
      2   3 <- see 3
       \
        5   <- see 5     (nothing on the right at this level, so 5 shows)
List<Integer> rightSideView(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return res;
    Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.offer(root);
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int size = q.size();
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            TreeNode node = q.poll();
            if (i == size - 1) res.add(node.val);
            if (node.left != null) q.offer(node.left);
            if (node.right != null) q.offer(node.right);
        }
    }
    return res;
}

DFS alternative: visit right child first; the first node seen at each new depth (depth == res.size()) is visible.

Maximum Width of Binary Tree (LC 662)

Key insight: number nodes like a heap — left child 2i, right child 2i + 1; width of a level = last index - first index + 1. Re-base indices per level to avoid overflow.

  index numbering (heap style, 0-based per level after re-basing)

  level 0:            1(0)                   width = 1
                    /      \
  level 1:      3(0)        2(1)             width = 2
               /    \           \
  level 2:  5(0)   3(1)   .      9(3)        width = 3 - 0 + 1 = 4  (gaps count)

  children of index i:  2i and 2i+1
int widthOfBinaryTree(TreeNode root) {
    record Item(TreeNode node, long idx) {}
    Deque<Item> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.offer(new Item(root, 0));
    int best = 0;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int size = q.size();
        long first = q.peekFirst().idx(), last = q.peekLast().idx();
        best = (int) Math.max(best, last - first + 1);
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            Item it = q.poll();
            long idx = it.idx() - first;               // re-base: level starts at 0
            if (it.node().left != null) q.offer(new Item(it.node().left, 2 * idx));
            if (it.node().right != null) q.offer(new Item(it.node().right, 2 * idx + 1));
        }
    }
    return best;
}

O(n) time, O(width) space.

Trap: Without re-basing, indices double every level and overflow long on a 64+ deep skewed path. Subtract the level's first index before computing children.

Vertical Order Traversal (LC 987)

Key insight: give each node a (column, row); root is (0, 0), left child column - 1, right child column + 1. Sort by column, then row, then value.

              3 (c0,r0)
            /          \
     9 (c-1,r1)      20 (c1,r1)
                   /          \
            15 (c0,r2)      7 (c2,r2)

  columns:  -1: [9]    0: [3, 15]    1: [20]    2: [7]
List<List<Integer>> verticalTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    List<int[]> nodes = new ArrayList<>();           // {col, row, val}
    collect(root, 0, 0, nodes);
    nodes.sort((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])
                       : a[1] != b[1] ? Integer.compare(a[1], b[1])
                       : Integer.compare(a[2], b[2]));
    List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
    int prevCol = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
    for (int[] n : nodes) {
        if (n[0] != prevCol) { res.add(new ArrayList<>()); prevCol = n[0]; }
        res.get(res.size() - 1).add(n[2]);
    }
    return res;
}
void collect(TreeNode node, int col, int row, List<int[]> nodes) {
    if (node == null) return;
    nodes.add(new int[]{col, row, node.val});
    collect(node.left, col - 1, row + 1, nodes);
    collect(node.right, col + 1, row + 1, nodes);
}

O(n log n) time, O(n) space. LC 314 (premium) is the easier version: BFS order within a column, no value tie-break; use a TreeMap<Integer, List<Integer>> filled during BFS.

Remember: Level problem = BFS + size. Width = heap indices 2i, 2i+1. Vertical = (col, row) coordinates then sort.

7.8 Lowest Common Ancestor

In plain words: The LCA of p and q is the deepest node with both of them below it (a node counts as its own ancestor). In a BST, go left while both values are smaller, right while both are bigger; where they split, stop. In a plain tree, the node whose left and right sides both report "found" is the answer.

Analogy: Your shared grandparent with a cousin: the first person up both family lines, not the great-grandparent above them.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/lca.html

Pattern: LCA — If you see: "lowest common ancestor", "distance between two nodes", "first shared manager" → think: bottom-up "did I find p or q below me?" (binary tree) or "split point" (BST). Time O(n) / O(h).

LCA of a Binary Tree (LC 236)

Key insight: return the node if it is p or q; if both sides return non-null, this node is the split point, so it is the LCA.

Step by step:

  1. If the node is null, p or q, return it.
  2. Recurse left and right.
  3. If both sides returned non-null, p and q are on different sides: return this node.
  4. Otherwise return the side that is non-null (or null).
              3                  find LCA(5, 4)
            /   \
           5     1               at 5: node == p -> return 5 immediately
          / \   / \              (4 is under 5, so 5 is the answer anyway)
         6   2 0   8
            / \                  find LCA(6, 4):
           7   4                 at 2: left null, right 4 -> return 4
                                 at 5: left 6, right 4 -> both! return 5
TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (root == null || root == p || root == q) return root;
    TreeNode l = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q);
    TreeNode r = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q);
    if (l != null && r != null) return root;   // p and q on different sides
    return l != null ? l : r;                  // pass up whichever was found
}

O(n) time, O(h) space. Assumes both p and q exist in the tree (LC guarantees it). If they might not, count how many you found.

LCA of a BST (LC 235)

Key insight: walk from the root; if both are smaller go left, both larger go right, otherwise this node splits them.

           6               LCA(2, 8): 2 < 6 < 8 -> split at 6
         /   \             LCA(2, 4): both < 6 go left; at 2: 2 == p -> split at 2
        2     8
       / \   / \
      0   4 7   9
TreeNode lowestCommonAncestorBST(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null) {
        if (p.val < cur.val && q.val < cur.val) cur = cur.left;
        else if (p.val > cur.val && q.val > cur.val) cur = cur.right;
        else return cur;
    }
    return null;
}

O(h) time, O(1) space.

Tip: Distance between two nodes = depth(p) + depth(q) - 2 · depth(LCA). Interviewers like this follow-up.

7.9 Build, serialize, reshape

In plain words: These problems rebuild or rewrite a whole tree. The trick is always to find the root first (for example preorder[0]), split the rest into a left part and a right part, and let recursion build each part. A tree of 7 nodes is rebuilt with 7 calls.

Analogy: Rebuilding a family tree from two lists: one says who came first, the other says who stands to the left of whom, and together they fix every position.

Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder (LC 105)

Say: "Preorder's first element is the root; its position in inorder splits left subtree from right subtree, and the sizes tell me how to split preorder."

  preorder = [3, 9, 20, 15, 7]      inorder = [9, 3, 15, 20, 7]
              ^root                              ^ root at index 1 (from hash map)

  inorder:   [ 9 ] [3] [ 15  20  7 ]          left size = 1 - 0 = 1
              left  root  right

  preorder:  [3] [ 9 ] [ 20  15  7 ]          take 1 element after root for left,
             root left    right                the rest for right

  recurse:  left  -> pre [9],          in [9]          -> leaf 9
            right -> pre [20, 15, 7],  in [15, 20, 7]  -> root 20, left 15, right 7

  result:        3
                / \
               9   20
                  /  \
                 15   7

Key insight: a preorder pointer that just moves forward, plus a value-to-index map for inorder, gives O(n).

int pre = 0;
Map<Integer, Integer> inIdx = new HashMap<>();
TreeNode buildTree(int[] preorder, int[] inorder) {
    for (int i = 0; i < inorder.length; i++) inIdx.put(inorder[i], i);
    return build(preorder, 0, inorder.length - 1);
}
TreeNode build(int[] preorder, int lo, int hi) {   // inorder range [lo, hi]
    if (lo > hi) return null;
    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(preorder[pre++]);
    int mid = inIdx.get(root.val);
    root.left = build(preorder, lo, mid - 1);      // MUST build left first
    root.right = build(preorder, mid + 1, hi);
    return root;
}

O(n) time, O(n) space. Values must be unique.

Trap: Build the left subtree before the right: the shared pre pointer consumes preorder in root-left-right order. For postorder + inorder (LC 106), walk postorder from the end and build right first.

Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree (LC 297)

Key insight: preorder with a # marker for null is enough to rebuild the tree uniquely; deserialize by consuming tokens in the same preorder.

       1           serialize (preorder, # = null):
      / \          "1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#"
     2   3
        / \        deserialize: read 1 -> left: read 2 -> left #, right # ->
       4   5       right: read 3 -> left: 4(#,#) -> right: 5(#,#)
public class Codec {
    public String serialize(TreeNode root) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        write(root, sb);
        return sb.toString();
    }
    private void write(TreeNode node, StringBuilder sb) {
        if (node == null) { sb.append("#,"); return; }
        sb.append(node.val).append(',');
        write(node.left, sb);
        write(node.right, sb);
    }
    public TreeNode deserialize(String data) {
        Deque<String> tokens = new ArrayDeque<>(Arrays.asList(data.split(",")));
        return read(tokens);
    }
    private TreeNode read(Deque<String> tokens) {
        String t = tokens.poll();
        if (t.equals("#")) return null;
        TreeNode node = new TreeNode(Integer.parseInt(t));
        node.left = read(tokens);
        node.right = read(tokens);
        return node;
    }
}

O(n) both ways. BFS (LeetCode's own format) also works; preorder recursion is shorter to write on a whiteboard.

Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List (LC 114)

Key insight: for each node with a left child, find the rightmost node of the left subtree, hang the right subtree there, move left to right. O(1) space (Morris-like).

  step 0          step 1 (at 1)            step 2 (at 2)          done
      1               1                        1                   1
     / \               \                        \                   \
    2   5               2                        2                   2
   / \   \             / \                        \                   \
  3   4   6           3   4                        3                   3
                           \                        \                   \
                            5                        4                   4
                             \                        \                   \
                              6                        5                   5
  rightmost of left(1) = 4;                             \                   \
  4.right = 5; 1.right = 2; 1.left = null                6                   6
void flatten(TreeNode root) {
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null) {
        if (cur.left != null) {
            TreeNode pre = cur.left;
            while (pre.right != null) pre = pre.right;   // rightmost of left subtree
            pre.right = cur.right;                        // hang right subtree there
            cur.right = cur.left;                         // move left subtree right
            cur.left = null;
        }
        cur = cur.right;
    }
}

O(n) time (each edge walked a constant number of times), O(1) space. Recursive alternative: process right, then left, keeping a prev pointer (reverse postorder).

7.10 Binary Search Trees

In plain words: A BST keeps everything smaller on the left and bigger on the right, for every node and its whole subtree. Searching for 7 from root 8 means: go left, and the whole right side is thrown away. A balanced BST of 1,000,000 values needs about 20 steps.

Analogy: Guess-my-number with "smaller / bigger" answers, written down as a tree.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/bst.html

Pattern: BST — If you see: "BST", "sorted order", "kth smallest", "successor", "closest value", "range" → think: in-order is sorted; use the ordering to discard half the tree. Time O(h) per search, O(n) for traversal.

The one rule

              8                     every node in LEFT subtree  <  node
            /   \                   every node in RIGHT subtree >  node
           3     10                 (whole subtree, not just the child!)
          / \      \
         1   6      14              in-order: 1 3 4 6 7 8 10 13 14   <- sorted
            / \    /
           4   7  13

Remember: BST + in-order = sorted array. Almost every BST problem is "do something to a sorted array, without building the array."

Validate Binary Search Tree (LC 98)

Key insight: pass down an open interval (min, max); each node must fit inside it. Going left tightens max, going right tightens min.

Step by step:

  1. Start at the root with the range (minus infinity, plus infinity).
  2. If the node's value is not strictly inside the range, return false.
  3. Check the left child with (min, node.val) and the right child with (node.val, max).
  4. A null node is always valid.
  The trap: checking only children
            5
           / \
          4   6          6 > 5 ok, 3 < 6 ok locally...
             / \
            3   7        ...but 3 is in 5's RIGHT subtree and 3 < 5 -> NOT a BST

  With bounds:  5 in (-inf, +inf)
                4 in (-inf, 5)      6 in (5, +inf)
                                    3 in (5, 6)   -> FAIL
boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root) { return valid(root, null, null); }
boolean valid(TreeNode node, Integer min, Integer max) {
    if (node == null) return true;
    if (min != null && node.val <= min) return false;
    if (max != null && node.val >= max) return false;
    return valid(node.left, min, node.val) && valid(node.right, node.val, max);
}

O(n) time, O(h) space. Alternative: iterative in-order, check every value is strictly greater than the previous.

Trap: Two traps. (1) Only comparing a node to its children (picture above). (2) Using Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE as the initial bounds — a node with value Integer.MAX_VALUE then fails. Use null (or long bounds).

Kth Smallest Element in a BST (LC 230)

Key insight: iterative in-order; stop at the kth pop.

int kthSmallest(TreeNode root, int k) {
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (true) {
        while (cur != null) { stack.push(cur); cur = cur.left; }
        cur = stack.pop();
        if (--k == 0) return cur.val;
        cur = cur.right;
    }
}

O(h + k) time, O(h) space. Follow-up "tree changes often": store subtree size in each node; then go left if k <= size(left), else go right with k - size(left) - 1 — O(h) per query.

Search, Insert and Delete in a BST (LC 700, 701, 450)

Key insight: search and insert follow one path down. Delete has three cases.

  DELETE cases                         delete 3 from:      8
  1. leaf            -> return null                       / \
  2. one child       -> return that child                3   10
  3. two children    -> copy successor (min of right)    / \
                        into node, delete successor     1   6
                        from right subtree                 / \
                                                          4   7
  successor of 3 = min(right subtree) = 4
  copy 4 into node 3, then delete 4 from the right subtree (it is a leaf)

  result:      8
              / \
             4   10
            / \
           1   6
                \
                 7
TreeNode searchBST(TreeNode root, int val) {
    while (root != null && root.val != val)
        root = val < root.val ? root.left : root.right;
    return root;
}

TreeNode insertIntoBST(TreeNode root, int val) {
    if (root == null) return new TreeNode(val);
    if (val < root.val) root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, val);
    else root.right = insertIntoBST(root.right, val);
    return root;
}

TreeNode deleteNode(TreeNode root, int key) {
    if (root == null) return null;
    if (key < root.val) root.left = deleteNode(root.left, key);
    else if (key > root.val) root.right = deleteNode(root.right, key);
    else {
        if (root.left == null) return root.right;      // cases 1 and 2
        if (root.right == null) return root.left;
        TreeNode succ = root.right;                     // case 3
        while (succ.left != null) succ = succ.left;
        root.val = succ.val;
        root.right = deleteNode(root.right, succ.val);
    }
    return root;
}

All O(h).

Tip: "Return the (possibly new) subtree root and reassign it" — root.left = insert(root.left, val) — is the cleanest way to write any recursive tree modification. No parent pointers needed.

Convert Sorted Array to BST (LC 108)

Key insight: the middle element is the root; recurse on each half. Gives a height-balanced tree.

  nums = [-10, -3, 0, 5, 9]
                   ^ mid -> root 0
          [-10,-3]      [5, 9]
             ^mid=-10      ^mid=5        ->        0
               [-3]          [9]                  / \
                                               -10   5
                                                 \    \
                                                 -3    9
TreeNode sortedArrayToBST(int[] nums) { return make(nums, 0, nums.length - 1); }
TreeNode make(int[] nums, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo > hi) return null;
    int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(nums[mid]);
    root.left = make(nums, lo, mid - 1);
    root.right = make(nums, mid + 1, hi);
    return root;
}

O(n) time, O(log n) stack.

Binary Search Tree Iterator (LC 173)

Key insight: the iterative in-order loop cut into pieces. The stack holds the "left spine" still to visit; next() pops one node and pushes the left spine of its right child.

  tree:     7               init: push left spine of 7 -> stack [7, 3]
           / \              next() -> pop 3, right null       -> 3, stack [7]
          3   15            next() -> pop 7, push spine(15)   -> 7, stack [15, 9]
             /  \           next() -> pop 9                   -> 9, stack [15]
            9    20         next() -> pop 15, push spine(20)  -> 15, stack [20]
                            next() -> pop 20                  -> 20, stack []
class BSTIterator {
    private final Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    public BSTIterator(TreeNode root) { pushLeft(root); }
    public int next() {
        TreeNode node = stack.pop();
        pushLeft(node.right);
        return node.val;
    }
    public boolean hasNext() { return !stack.isEmpty(); }
    private void pushLeft(TreeNode node) {
        while (node != null) { stack.push(node); node = node.left; }
    }
}

next() is O(1) amortized (each node pushed and popped once), space O(h).

Inorder Successor in BST (LC 285)

Key insight: walk from the root; whenever you go left, the current node is a candidate (it is bigger than p); the last candidate is the successor.

  successor of 6 in:      8            at 8: 6 < 8 -> candidate 8, go left
                         / \           at 3: 6 > 3 -> go right
                        3   10         at 6: 6 = 6 -> go right
                       / \             at 7: 6 < 7 -> candidate 7, go left -> null
                      1   6            answer = 7
                           \
                            7
TreeNode inorderSuccessor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p) {
    TreeNode succ = null, cur = root;
    while (cur != null) {
        if (p.val < cur.val) { succ = cur; cur = cur.left; }
        else cur = cur.right;
    }
    return succ;
}

O(h) time, O(1) space. Predecessor is the mirror: candidate when going right on p.val > cur.val.

Remember: Successor = "the last node where I turned left". Predecessor = "the last node where I turned right".

Trap: In a BST problem, an O(n) in-order solution is usually accepted but the interviewer wants O(h). Say both, write the O(h) one.

7.11 Morris traversal (O(1) space in-order)

In plain words: Normal in-order needs a stack to find the way back up. Morris borrows an empty right pointer in the left subtree as a temporary "return here" arrow, uses it once, and then removes it. No stack, so O(1) extra space, still O(n) time.

Analogy: Leaving a sticky note on the last shelf of an aisle that says "go back to the main corridor", and peeling it off when you use it.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/tree-traversals.html

Say: "Morris traversal threads each node's in-order predecessor back to it, so I can return without a stack, then removes the thread on the second visit."

  Visit 4's left subtree; predecessor of 4 is 3 (rightmost of left subtree).
  first time at 4:  3.right == null -> set thread 3.right = 4, go left
  ... visit 1, 2, 3 ...  3.right is the thread -> back to 4
  second time at 4: 3.right == 4  -> remove thread, visit 4, go right

          4                 4
         /                 / ^
        2       ->        2  |
       / \               / \ |
      1   3             1   3   (3.right temporarily points to 4)
List<Integer> morrisInorder(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null) {
        if (cur.left == null) {
            res.add(cur.val);
            cur = cur.right;                 // may follow a thread back up
        } else {
            TreeNode pre = cur.left;
            while (pre.right != null && pre.right != cur) pre = pre.right;
            if (pre.right == null) {         // first visit: make the thread
                pre.right = cur;
                cur = cur.left;
            } else {                         // second visit: remove it
                pre.right = null;
                res.add(cur.val);
                cur = cur.right;
            }
        }
    }
    return res;
}

O(n) time, O(1) extra space. It temporarily modifies the tree, so mention that it is not safe under concurrent reads. Bring it up when the interviewer asks "can you do it without the stack?" (Kth Smallest, Recover BST LC 99).

7.12 Balanced BSTs and TreeMap

In plain words: If you insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 into a plain BST it becomes a line and search costs O(n). Balanced trees (AVL, red-black) rotate nodes after each insert so the height stays about log n. Java's TreeMap and TreeSet are red-black trees.

Analogy: A bookshelf that is automatically re-spread after every new book so no single end gets piled up.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/bst.html

You will not implement AVL or Red-Black trees in an interview. Know what to say.

Tree Rule What to say
AVL Heights of children differ by at most 1 Stricter balance, faster lookups, more rotations on insert/delete
Red-Black Colour rules; longest path at most 2x shortest Fewer rotations; used by Java TreeMap/TreeSet and HashMap buckets with 8+ entries
B-tree / B+ tree Many keys per node, all leaves at the same depth Disk-friendly; database indexes (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB) 
  Rotation fixes a lean (right rotation at 3):

        3                 2
       /                 / \
      2        ->       1   3
     /
    1
  Inserting 1, 2, 3 in order into a plain BST gives a line; a balanced tree rotates.

TreeMap / TreeSet cheat sheet (all O(log n))

Call Returns
floorKey(x) largest key <= x
ceilingKey(x) smallest key >= x
lowerKey(x) largest key < x
higherKey(x) smallest key > x
firstKey() / lastKey() min / max
pollFirstEntry() remove and return min
headMap(x) / tailMap(x) / subMap(a, b) views of ranges

Use it when a problem needs "the nearest value below/above x" while values are being inserted: My Calendar I (LC 729), Contains Duplicate III (LC 220), Time Based Key-Value Store (LC 981), stock price tracking.

// My Calendar I (LC 729): no overlapping bookings [start, end)
class MyCalendar {
    private final TreeMap<Integer, Integer> cal = new TreeMap<>();   // start -> end
    public boolean book(int start, int end) {
        Integer prev = cal.floorKey(start);     // booking starting at or before me
        Integer next = cal.ceilingKey(start);   // booking starting at or after me
        if (prev != null && cal.get(prev) > start) return false;
        if (next != null && next < end) return false;
        cal.put(start, end);
        return true;
    }
}

Trap: floorKey returns Integer and returns null when nothing qualifies. Unboxing it into int throws NullPointerException. Always null-check.

7.13 Segment tree and Fenwick tree (range queries with updates)

In plain words: Prefix sums answer "sum of positions 2 to 5" in O(1) but one change costs O(n). A segment tree stores sums of halves, quarters and so on, so both a query and an update touch only about log n boxes: about 20 for a million numbers.

Analogy: A company's budget report: each manager keeps their team's total, so one salary change updates only the managers above that person.

Pattern: Range query + point update — If you see: "sum/min/max of range [l, r]" AND "update index i" interleaved, many queries → think: Fenwick tree (sum) or segment tree (any associative op). O(log n) per op, O(n) space.

Why: prefix sums answer range sums in O(1) but an update costs O(n). Plain arrays update in O(1) but query in O(n). These trees make both O(log n).

Segment tree picture

  nums = [2, 1, 5, 3]          each node stores the sum of its range

                     [0..3] = 11
                    /           \
            [0..1] = 3        [2..3] = 8
             /     \           /     \
        [0]=2    [1]=1     [2]=5    [3]=3

  query sum(1..3): [1]=1 + [2..3]=8 = 9        (visit O(log n) nodes)
  update nums[2]=7: change [2], [2..3], [0..3] (one root-to-leaf path)

  Array layout (1-indexed, size 2n with the iterative version):
  tree[n + i] = nums[i] (leaves); tree[i] = tree[2i] + tree[2i+1]

Range Sum Query - Mutable (LC 307) with an iterative segment tree

class NumArray {
    private final int n;
    private final int[] tree;
    public NumArray(int[] nums) {
        n = nums.length;
        tree = new int[2 * n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) tree[n + i] = nums[i];          // leaves
        for (int i = n - 1; i > 0; i--) tree[i] = tree[2 * i] + tree[2 * i + 1];
    }
    public void update(int i, int val) {
        i += n;
        tree[i] = val;
        for (i /= 2; i > 0; i /= 2) tree[i] = tree[2 * i] + tree[2 * i + 1];
    }
    public int sumRange(int l, int r) {          // inclusive [l, r]
        int sum = 0;
        for (l += n, r += n + 1; l < r; l /= 2, r /= 2) {   // half-open [l, r)
            if ((l & 1) == 1) sum += tree[l++];  // l is a right child: take it alone
            if ((r & 1) == 1) sum += tree[--r];  // r-1 is a left child: take it alone
        }
        return sum;
    }
}
  Trace: nums = [2, 1, 5, 3], n = 4
  tree index:  1   2   3   4   5   6   7
  tree value: 11   3   8   2   1   5   3       (4..7 are leaves)

  sumRange(1, 3): l = 5, r = 8
    l=5 odd -> sum = 1, l = 6        r=8 even
    l = 3, r = 4
    l=3 odd -> sum = 1 + 8 = 9, l = 4   r=4 even
    l = 2, r = 2 -> stop.  answer 9

Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree)

Say: "A Fenwick tree stores, at index i, the sum of the last lowbit(i) elements, where lowbit(i) = i & -i; update climbs by adding lowbit, query descends by subtracting it."

  1-indexed. i & -i = lowest set bit = how many elements index i covers.

  i (binary)   covers         i & -i
  1  (0001)    [1]            1
  2  (0010)    [1..2]         2
  3  (0011)    [3]            1
  4  (0100)    [1..4]         4
  5  (0101)    [5]            1
  6  (0110)    [5..6]         2
  7  (0111)    [7]            1
  8  (1000)    [1..8]         8

  prefix(7) = bit[7] + bit[6] + bit[4]      (7 -> 6 -> 4 -> 0, subtract lowbit)
  update(3) touches bit[3], bit[4], bit[8]  (3 -> 4 -> 8, add lowbit)
class Fenwick {
    private final int[] bit;                       // 1-indexed
    Fenwick(int n) { bit = new int[n + 1]; }
    void add(int i, int delta) {                   // i is 0-based outside
        for (i++; i < bit.length; i += i & -i) bit[i] += delta;
    }
    int prefix(int i) {                            // sum of [0..i]
        int s = 0;
        for (i++; i > 0; i -= i & -i) s += bit[i];
        return s;
    }
    int range(int l, int r) { return prefix(r) - (l == 0 ? 0 : prefix(l - 1)); }
}
// LC 307 with Fenwick: keep nums[];
// update(i, val) -> add(i, val - nums[i]); nums[i] = val.
Prefix sum array Fenwick Segment tree
Build O(n) O(n log n) O(n)
Point update O(n) O(log n) O(log n)
Range query O(1) O(log n) O(log n)
Supports min/max no awkward yes
Range update no with tricks lazy propagation

Remember: Static array + range sum → prefix sums. Updates + range sum → Fenwick (i & -i). Updates + min/max or anything fancy → segment tree.

Tip: Fenwick also solves "count of smaller numbers after self" (LC 315) and inversion counting: iterate from the right, query how many smaller values were added, then add the current value (compress values to ranks first).

7.14 Which tree technique?

7.z Chapter cheat sheet

Trigger Pattern Template one-liner Complexity
Depth, height, size Bottom-up return 1 + max(f(l), f(r)) O(n) / O(h)
Running state on path Top-down f(child, state') O(n) / O(h)
Longest / max path anywhere Global + one arm best = max(best, l+r+v); return v+max(l,r) O(n) / O(h)
Balanced check -1 sentinel if (l==-1 || r==-1 || abs(l-r)>1) return -1 O(n)
Level, row, right view BFS size = q.size(); for i < size O(n) / O(w)
Width Heap indices children 2i, 2i+1, re-base per level O(n)
Count paths summing to k Prefix map on tree seen[cur-k], backtrack seen[cur]-- O(n)
LCA binary tree Found-below both sides non-null → me O(n)
LCA BST / successor Walk down split point / last left turn O(h)
Build from pre + in Root + index map pre++, split at inIdx[root] O(n)
Serialize Preorder with # read tokens in same order O(n)
Validate BST Bounds valid(l, min, v) && valid(r, v, max) O(n)
Kth smallest / iterator Iterative in-order dive left, pop, go right O(h + k)
Nearest key with inserts TreeMap floorKey / ceilingKey O(log n)
Range sum + updates Fenwick / segment tree i += i & -i / tree[n+i] O(log n)

Never forget

  • Ask "what do I need from children, what do I return, what do I pass down?" before coding.
  • Write the null base case first and decide what an empty tree returns.
  • Depth is from the root down, height is from the leaves up; check if the problem counts nodes or edges.
  • Iterative in-order: while (cur != null || !stack.isEmpty()) — dive left, pop, go right.
  • BFS: store q.size() before the inner loop.
  • ArrayDeque rejects null; check children before pushing.
  • Path can bend: global gets l + v + r, parent gets v + max(l, r); clamp negative arms to 0.
  • Max path sum starts at Integer.MIN_VALUE, not 0.
  • Path Sum II: copy the path (new ArrayList<>(path)) and backtrack.
  • Path Sum III: prefix map seeded with {0: 1}, decrement on the way back up, use long.
  • Validate BST with (min, max) bounds, not child comparisons; use null or long bounds.
  • BST in-order is sorted; successor = last left turn.
  • Build from preorder + inorder: left before right; postorder + inorder: right before left.
  • Width: re-base indices per level or they overflow.
  • Recursion depth = tree height; a skewed tree of 10^5 nodes can overflow the stack — offer iterative.

8. Heaps, Priority Queues and Tries

Two data structures that turn brute force into fast answers. A heap gives you the smallest (or largest) item in O(1) and lets you add or remove in O(log n): it is the tool for "top K", "running median", "merge K sorted" and "what runs next". A trie stores strings by shared prefixes: it is the tool for "starts with", autocomplete and searching many words at once.

8.1 The heap: a tree stored in an array

In plain words: A min-heap is a tree where every parent is smaller than its children, so the smallest value sits at the top. It is stored in an array: children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. Insert adds at the end and swaps upward; removing the top moves the last value to the root and swaps it downward — about log₂ n swaps, 20 for a million items.

Analogy: an org chart where every boss outranks the people below; a new hire who outranks their boss swaps places until the order is right.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/heap.html

Say this aloud first: "A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array, where every parent is smaller than its children in a min-heap; the minimum is always at index 0."

  Min-heap as a tree                    Same heap as an array

            [1]                         index:  0   1   2   3   4   5
           /   \                        value:  1   3   2   7   4   5
        [3]     [2]
        / \     /                       parent(i)     = (i - 1) / 2
      [7] [4] [5]                       leftChild(i)  = 2i + 1
                                        rightChild(i) = 2i + 2
  Heap property: parent <= children.
  NOT sorted: 3 and 2 are siblings in any order, 7 sits below 3 but above nothing.
  Complete tree -> no gaps in the array -> height = floor(log2 n).
Operation Cost How
peek() O(1) heap[0]
offer(x) O(log n) append at end, sift up
poll() O(log n) move last to root, sift down
build from n items O(n) sift down from the last parent to 0
remove(x) arbitrary O(n) linear search, then sift
contains(x) O(n) linear search

Sift up (insert) trace

  offer(0) into [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5]

  append at index 6:       [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5, 0]       parent(6) = 2 (value 2)
  0 < 2 -> swap:           [1, 3, 0, 7, 4, 5, 2]       parent(2) = 0 (value 1)
  0 < 1 -> swap:           [0, 3, 1, 7, 4, 5, 2]       at root -> stop

            [1]                   [1]                   [0]
           /   \                 /   \                 /   \
        [3]     [2]    ->     [3]     [0]    ->     [3]     [1]
        / \     / \           / \     / \           / \     / \
      [7] [4] [5] (0)       [7] [4] [5] [2]       [7] [4] [5] [2]

Sift down (poll) trace

  poll() from [0, 3, 1, 7, 4, 5, 2]  -> returns 0

  move last (2) to root:   [2, 3, 1, 7, 4, 5]          children of 0: 3 and 1
  smaller child 1 < 2:     [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5]          children of 2: 5 (index 5)
  5 > 2 -> stop.

  Rule: swap with the SMALLER child, otherwise the smaller child would end up
  below the larger one and break the property.

Minimal heap implementation

You rarely write one, but "implement a heap" does come up, and writing it once makes the cost model stick.

Step by step

  1. Keep the values in an array list; index 0 is the root.
  2. push: add the value at the end, then swap it with its parent (i - 1) / 2 while it is smaller.
  3. poll: remember the root, move the last value to index 0 and shrink the list.
  4. Sift down: swap with the smaller child (2i + 1 or 2i + 2) while that child is smaller.
  5. Return the remembered root.
class MinHeap {
    private int[] a = new int[16];
    private int size = 0;

    void offer(int x) {
        if (size == a.length) a = Arrays.copyOf(a, size * 2);
        a[size] = x;
        int i = size++;
        while (i > 0 && a[(i - 1) / 2] > a[i]) {        // sift up
            swap(i, (i - 1) / 2);
            i = (i - 1) / 2;
        }
    }
    int poll() {
        int top = a[0];
        a[0] = a[--size];
        siftDown(0);
        return top;
    }
    int peek() { return a[0]; }

    private void siftDown(int i) {
        while (true) {
            int l = 2 * i + 1, r = 2 * i + 2, min = i;
            if (l < size && a[l] < a[min]) min = l;
            if (r < size && a[r] < a[min]) min = r;
            if (min == i) return;
            swap(i, min);
            i = min;
        }
    }
    static MinHeap heapify(int[] nums) {             // O(n) build
        MinHeap h = new MinHeap();
        h.a = Arrays.copyOf(nums, Math.max(16, nums.length));
        h.size = nums.length;
        for (int i = h.size / 2 - 1; i >= 0; i--) h.siftDown(i);
        return h;
    }
    private void swap(int i, int j) { int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t; }
}

Why heapify is O(n), not O(n log n)

  level (from bottom)   nodes        max sift-down distance     work
  leaves                ~n/2         0                          0
  1 above leaves        ~n/4         1                          n/4
  2 above               ~n/8         2                          2n/8
  3 above               ~n/16        3                          3n/16
  ...
  total = n * (1/4 + 2/8 + 3/16 + ...) = n * 1 = O(n)

  Most nodes are near the bottom and barely move. Inserting one by one is O(n log n)
  because each insert can sift all the way up.

Remember: Parent (i-1)/2, children 2i+1, 2i+2. Insert sifts UP, poll sifts DOWN, heapify from the middle is O(n).

8.2 Java PriorityQueue

In plain words: PriorityQueue is Java's ready-made heap. By default poll() returns the smallest value; pass a comparator such as Collections.reverseOrder() to get the largest. offer and poll cost O(log n), peek costs O(1).

Analogy: a hospital waiting room where the most urgent patient is always called next, no matter when they arrived.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/heap.html

PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();               // default: min
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap2 = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(b, a));

PriorityQueue<int[]> byFirst = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
PriorityQueue<int[]> byDist = new PriorityQueue<>(
        Comparator.comparingInt((int[] p) -> p[0] * p[0] + p[1] * p[1]));

record Item(String word, int freq) {}
PriorityQueue<Item> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(
        Comparator.comparingInt(Item::freq).thenComparing(Item::word));
Method Does Cost
offer(x) / add(x) insert O(log n)
poll() remove min, null if empty O(log n)
peek() min, null if empty O(1)
remove(x) remove one equal element O(n)
size(), isEmpty() O(1)
new PriorityQueue<>(collection) heapify O(n)

Trap: (a, b) -> a - b overflows. With a = Integer.MIN_VALUE and b = 1, a - b wraps to a large positive number and the order is wrong. Always use Integer.compare(a, b) or Comparator.comparingInt.

Trap: Iterating a PriorityQueue (for-each, toString, stream) does not give sorted order; only repeated poll() does. Also, mutating a field used by the comparator after insertion corrupts the heap: remove, change, re-insert.

Tip: Java has no decrease-key. For Dijkstra-style problems insert a new entry and skip stale ones when polled (if (d > dist[u]) continue;). This "lazy deletion" idea also powers Sliding Window Median.

8.3 Top-K: the size-K heap

In plain words: To keep the 3 largest of [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4, 8], hold at most 3 numbers in a min-heap. Each new number joins; if there are 4, remove the smallest. At the end the heap is {5, 6, 8} and its top, 5, is the 3rd largest. Cost O(n log k).

Analogy: a talent show with 3 finalist chairs: a better act takes the chair of the weakest finalist.

Watch it: animated version — https://abinesh1006.github.io/prep/visual/lessons/top-k.html

Pattern: Top K — If you see: "k largest", "k most frequent", "k closest", "kth largest" → think: keep a heap of size k with the opposite order: a min-heap for the k largest (the root is the weakest of the winners, ready to be kicked out). Time O(n log k), space O(k).

  k = 3 largest of [5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 2, 8]     min-heap (root first)

  add 5            [5]
  add 1            [1, 5]
  add 9            [1, 5, 9]            size 3 = k
  add 3            [1, 3, 5, 9] -> poll 1 -> [3, 5, 9]
  add 7            [3, 5, 7, 9] -> poll 3 -> [5, 7, 9]
  add 2            [2, 5, 7, 9] -> poll 2 -> [5, 7, 9]
  add 8            [5, 7, 8, 9] -> poll 5 -> [7, 8, 9]

  heap = the 3 largest {7, 8, 9}; root 7 = 3rd largest
  The root is the bouncer: anything smaller than it never stays.
// Template: k largest by some score
PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();      // min-heap for LARGEST
for (int x : nums) {
    heap.offer(x);
    if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();                       // evict the weakest
}
// heap.peek() is the kth largest; the heap holds the top k

Remember: k LARGEST → MIN-heap. k SMALLEST / CLOSEST → MAX-heap. The heap holds the winners; the root is the first to be thrown out.

Kth Largest Element in an Array (LC 215)

Key insight: size-k min-heap; the root is the answer. Mention Quickselect as the O(n) average alternative.

Step by step

  1. Create an empty min-heap.
  2. For each number, offer it to the heap.
  3. If the heap now holds more than k numbers, poll the smallest.
  4. After the loop the heap holds the k largest; its root is the kth largest.
int findKthLargest(int[] nums, int k) {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();
    for (int x : nums) {
        heap.offer(x);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();
    }
    return heap.peek();
}

O(n log k) time, O(k) space.

// Quickselect: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst; randomize the pivot
int findKthLargestQS(int[] nums, int k) {
    int target = nums.length - k, lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1;   // kth largest index
    Random rnd = new Random();
    while (true) {
        int p = partition(nums, lo, hi, lo + rnd.nextInt(hi - lo + 1));
        if (p == target) return nums[p];
        if (p < target) lo = p + 1; else hi = p - 1;
    }
}
int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi, int pivotIdx) {   // Lomuto
    int pivot = a[pivotIdx];
    swap(a, pivotIdx, hi);
    int store = lo;
