  • Effects are for syncing with the outside world; derive the rest during render.
  • Server state belongs in React Query, not useState or Redux.

14. Backend: REST APIs, Spring Boot and Databases

Backend rounds probe whether you can design a clean API, explain what Spring does behind the annotations, write SQL without an ORM, and reason about consistency under concurrency. This chapter goes from the wire (HTTP) to the disk (indexes, transactions) and ends with 45 interview Q&A.

14.1 REST API design

REST models the domain as resources (nouns) addressed by URLs and manipulated with a small set of HTTP verbs.

GET    /orgs/{org}/invoices                 list (filter, sort, page)
GET    /orgs/{org}/invoices/{id}            read one
POST   /orgs/{org}/invoices                 create   -> 201 + Location header
PUT    /orgs/{org}/invoices/{id}            replace whole resource
PATCH  /orgs/{org}/invoices/{id}            partial update
DELETE /orgs/{org}/invoices/{id}            delete   -> 204
POST   /orgs/{org}/invoices/{id}/approve    action that is not CRUD (verb as sub-resource)
GET    /orgs/{org}/invoices/{id}/lines      nested collection

Remember: Nouns in the path, verbs in the method, plural collections, nest at most one or two levels, filters in the query string.

Methods: safe and idempotent

Method Safe (no side effect) Idempotent (repeat = same result) Body
GET yes yes no
HEAD / OPTIONS yes yes no
PUT no yes yes
DELETE no yes usually no
POST no no yes
PATCH no not guaranteed yes

Making POST idempotent: the client sends Idempotency-Key: <uuid>; the server stores key → response for 24 h and returns the stored response on retry. Payment APIs (Stripe, Paddle) work this way.

Status codes

Code Meaning When
200 OK success with body GET, PUT, PATCH
201 Created resource created POST, with Location
202 Accepted queued for async work long-running job
204 No Content success, no body DELETE
301 / 308 permanent redirect moved URL (308 keeps method)
304 Not Modified cached copy still valid If-None-Match + ETag
400 Bad Request malformed / validation failed bad JSON, missing field
401 Unauthorized not authenticated missing/expired token
403 Forbidden authenticated, not allowed wrong role or tenant
404 Not Found no such resource also to hide existence
405 Method Not Allowed verb not supported
409 Conflict state conflict duplicate, version mismatch
412 Precondition Failed If-Match ETag mismatch optimistic concurrency
415 Unsupported Media Type wrong Content-Type
422 Unprocessable Entity well-formed but semantically invalid business rule failed
429 Too Many Requests rate limited with Retry-After
500 Internal Server Error bug
502 / 503 / 504 bad gateway / unavailable / gateway timeout upstream problems

Trap: 401 vs 403 — 401 means "who are you?", 403 means "I know you, and no."

Pagination: offset vs cursor

OFFSET:  GET /items?page=3&size=20   ->  SELECT ... ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40
         DB still walks 40 rows, then returns 20.  Page 5000 walks 100,000 rows.
         Insert during paging -> row shifts -> duplicate or skipped item.

CURSOR:  GET /items?after=eyJpZCI6MTAwfQ&size=20
         cursor = base64({ "id": 100 })
         ->  SELECT ... WHERE id > 100 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20      (index seek, O(log n))
         response: { items: [...], nextCursor: "eyJpZCI6MTIwfQ" }
Offset Cursor (keyset)
Jump to page N yes no
Deep page cost grows linearly constant
Stable under inserts no yes
Best for admin tables with page numbers feeds, infinite scroll, exports

Tip: For keyset on a non-unique sort column, use a tuple: WHERE (created_at, id) < (:ts, :id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC.

Versioning and error envelope

Strategy Example Note
URL path /v1/orders simplest, most common, cache-friendly
Header Accept: application/vnd.acme.v2+json clean URLs, harder to test
Query ?version=2 rare

Only bump the version for breaking changes; adding fields is not breaking. A consistent envelope:

{
  "success": false,
  "data": null,
  "error": { "code": "INVOICE_NOT_FOUND", "message": "Invoice 42 not found",
             "fields": [{ "field": "amount", "message": "must be positive" }],
             "traceId": "a1b2c3" }
}

Spring Boot 3 also supports RFC 7807/9457 ProblemDetail (type, title, status, detail, instance).

14.2 HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3

HTTP/1.1  one request at a time per TCP connection (browsers open ~6)
          conn1: [req A ----resp A][req B ----resp B]
          conn2: [req C ----resp C]
HTTP/2    one TCP connection, many streams multiplexed as binary frames
          conn : [A1][B1][C1][A2][C2][B2] ...  but one lost TCP packet stalls ALL streams
HTTP/3    QUIC over UDP: streams are independent; loss stalls only that stream
          + 0-RTT/1-RTT handshake (TLS 1.3 built in), connection migration (wifi -> 4G)
HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3
Transport TCP TCP QUIC (UDP)
Format text binary frames binary frames
Multiplexing no (pipelining unused) yes yes
Head-of-line blocking HTTP level TCP level none across streams
Header compression no HPACK QPACK
TLS optional practically required built in (TLS 1.3)

14.3 What happens when you type a URL

Say: "DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP request, server work, response, then the browser's rendering pipeline."

Tip: Name the caches on the way: browser cache, OS DNS cache, resolver cache, CDN edge, reverse proxy, application cache (Redis), DB buffer pool.

14.4 Spring Boot request lifecycle

A request passes the servlet filter chain (Spring Security lives here), reaches the DispatcherServlet, which finds a handler, runs interceptors, converts the body, calls your controller and serialises the result.

Remember: Filter (servlet level, before Spring MVC) → Interceptor (around handler) → AOP advice (around bean methods). Security = filters.

Tip: Spring Boot 3.2+ with Java 21: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true runs each request on a virtual thread — blocking JDBC calls stop being a thread-pool bottleneck.

14.5 Dependency injection, beans and scopes

The container creates objects (beans), wires their dependencies, and manages their lifecycle so classes depend on interfaces, not on new.

@Service
public class InvoiceService {
    private final InvoiceRepository repo;          // final = immutable, testable
    private final Clock clock;
    public InvoiceService(InvoiceRepository repo, Clock clock) {   // constructor injection
        this.repo = repo; this.clock = clock;
    }
}
Injection Verdict
Constructor preferred: final fields, mandatory deps visible, easy unit tests, no reflection
Setter optional dependencies
Field @Autowired avoid: hidden deps, cannot be final, needs reflection in tests

Bean lifecycle

 scan @Component/@Bean -> BeanDefinition
   -> instantiate (constructor)
   -> inject dependencies
   -> Aware callbacks (BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware)
   -> BeanPostProcessor.before
   -> @PostConstruct / afterPropertiesSet
   -> BeanPostProcessor.after   <-- PROXIES are created here (@Transactional, @Async, AOP)
   -> READY (in use)
   -> @PreDestroy on shutdown
Scope One instance per Note
singleton (default) container must be stateless / thread-safe
prototype each injection / getBean container does not call destroy
request HTTP request web only, injected via proxy
session HTTP session web only
application ServletContext

Trap: Injecting a prototype into a singleton gives the singleton one prototype instance forever. Use ObjectProvider<T>.getObject() or @Lookup.

Trap: Two beans of the same type → NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Fix with @Primary or @Qualifier("name").

14.6 @Transactional and its proxy traps

@Transactional works through a proxy: the caller talks to a proxy that opens a transaction, calls your real method, then commits or rolls back.

 Controller ---> [ Proxy of InvoiceService ] ---> real InvoiceService.save()
                   begin tx                             |
                   call target ------------------------>|
                   commit / rollback  <-----------------+

 self-invocation:  real.save() -> this.audit()   <-- 'this' is the REAL object,
                                                      proxy bypassed, @Transactional IGNORED
Trap Why Fix
calling a @Transactional method from the same class bypasses the proxy move it to another bean, or inject self
method is private / final proxy cannot override make it public
checked exception does not roll back default rolls back on RuntimeException and Error only @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
catching the exception inside proxy never sees it rethrow, or setRollbackOnly()
REQUIRES_NEW inner method in same class self-invocation again separate bean
long transaction doing HTTP calls holds a DB connection and locks do remote calls outside the tx
@Transactional on controller wider than needed put it on service methods

Propagation

Propagation Behaviour
REQUIRED (default) join existing or start new
REQUIRES_NEW suspend current, always new (audit log that must persist)
NESTED savepoint inside current
SUPPORTS join if present, else non-transactional
MANDATORY must already exist, else exception
NOT_SUPPORTED / NEVER run without / fail if one exists

Remember: Proxy-based = public methods called from another bean, unchecked exceptions roll back. readOnly = true for queries (Hibernate skips dirty checking).

14.7 Validation and exception handling

public record CreateInvoice(
    @NotBlank String customer,
    @NotNull @Positive BigDecimal amount,
    @Size(max = 3) String currency,
    @NotEmpty List<@Valid Line> lines) {}

@PostMapping("/orgs/{org}/invoices")
public ResponseEntity<ApiResponse<InvoiceDto>> create(@PathVariable String org,
                                                      @Valid @RequestBody CreateInvoice req) {
    InvoiceDto dto = service.create(org, req);
    return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/orgs/" + org + "/invoices/" + dto.id()))
                         .body(ApiResponse.ok(dto));
}
@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalErrors {
    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    ResponseEntity<ApiResponse<Void>> invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) {
        var fields = e.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
            .map(f -> new FieldError(f.getField(), f.getDefaultMessage())).toList();
        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(ApiResponse.error("VALIDATION", "Invalid input", fields));
    }
    @ExceptionHandler(NotFoundException.class)
    ResponseEntity<ApiResponse<Void>> notFound(NotFoundException e) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(404).body(ApiResponse.error("NOT_FOUND", e.getMessage(), List.of()));
    }
    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    ResponseEntity<ApiResponse<Void>> unknown(Exception e) {
        log.error("Unhandled", e);                         // log the stack, hide it from the client
        return ResponseEntity.status(500).body(ApiResponse.error("INTERNAL", "Something went wrong", List.of()));
    }
}

Trap: @Valid on a nested object or list element is required for cascading validation. And path/query param constraints need @Validated on the controller class.

14.8 Security: sessions, JWT, OAuth2

Sessions vs tokens

Server session (cookie with session id) JWT bearer token
State server stores session (memory/Redis) stateless; claims inside the signed token
Revocation delete the session — instant hard: wait for expiry, or keep a denylist
Scaling needs sticky sessions or shared store any instance can verify with the public key
CSRF vulnerable (cookies auto-sent) immune if sent in Authorization header
XSS HttpOnly cookie not readable token readable if stored in JS-accessible storage
Size small id hundreds of bytes on every request

JWT structure and validation

eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9 . eyJzdWIiOiJ1MSIsInJvbGVzIjpbIkFETUlOIl0sImV4cCI6MTcwMH0 . SflKxw...
 header (alg, kid)       payload (sub, roles, iss, aud, exp, iat)                 signature
 base64url               base64url — NOT encrypted, anyone can read it            RS256(h.p)

 validate: signature with issuer public key (JWKS, by kid) -> exp/nbf -> iss -> aud

OAuth2 Authorization Code + PKCE (SPA login)

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .csrf(c -> c.disable())                                  // stateless bearer tokens
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers("/actuator/health", "/public/**").permitAll()
            .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/orgs/*/users/*").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))   // issuer-uri in yml
        .build();
}
OAuth2 term Meaning
Resource owner the user
Client the app (SPA, mobile, backend)
Authorization server issues tokens (Keycloak, Auth0, Okta)
Resource server your API, validates tokens
Scope what the token may do (read:invoices)
OIDC identity layer on top: id_token, /userinfo

Remember: Authentication = who you are (401). Authorization = what you may do (403). OAuth2 is delegated authorization; OIDC adds authentication.

Trap: JWT payload is only encoded, not encrypted — never put secrets in it. And always validate aud; a token issued for another app should be rejected.

Tip: Short access token (5–15 min) + rotating refresh token gives near-instant revocation without a per-request DB lookup.

14.9 SQL must-knows

Joins

  employees (e)          departments (d)
  id name   dept_id      id name
  1  Ann    10           10 Eng
  2  Bob    20           20 Sales
  3  Cid    NULL         30 Legal

 INNER JOIN on e.dept_id = d.id      -> Ann-Eng, Bob-Sales                  (matches only)
 LEFT JOIN  (employees left)         -> Ann-Eng, Bob-Sales, Cid-NULL        (all left rows)
 RIGHT JOIN (departments right)      -> Ann-Eng, Bob-Sales, NULL-Legal      (all right rows)
 FULL JOIN                           -> all four combinations above
 CROSS JOIN                          -> 3 x 3 = 9 rows
 SELF JOIN  e JOIN e m ON e.manager_id = m.id   -> employee with manager

      INNER          LEFT           RIGHT          FULL
     ( (##) )      (##(##) )      ( (##)##)      (##(##)##)

Trap: A WHERE d.name = 'Eng' after a LEFT JOIN silently turns it into an inner join (NULL rows fail the filter). Put the condition in the ON clause to keep unmatched rows.

Logical order of evaluation

 FROM / JOIN  ->  WHERE  ->  GROUP BY  ->  HAVING  ->  SELECT (window fns here)
   ->  DISTINCT  ->  ORDER BY  ->  LIMIT / OFFSET

That is why WHERE cannot use an aggregate (use HAVING) and cannot use a SELECT alias, but ORDER BY can.

Window functions

A window function computes over a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them, unlike GROUP BY.

SELECT name, dept, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER()   OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn,     -- 1,2,3,4
       RANK()         OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,    -- 1,2,2,4
       DENSE_RANK()   OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk,   -- 1,2,2,3
       SUM(salary)    OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hired)       AS running,
       LAG(salary)    OVER (ORDER BY hired)                         AS prev_salary,
       AVG(salary)    OVER (PARTITION BY dept)                      AS dept_avg
FROM employees;
salaries in dept: 900, 800, 800, 700
  ROW_NUMBER  1  2  3  4     unique always
  RANK        1  2  2  4     gap after tie
  DENSE_RANK  1  2  2  3     no gap

The 10 classic SQL interview queries

1. Nth highest salary (N = 2)

SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
-- or, returns NULL when absent:
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
-- general N with ties handled:
SELECT salary FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) r FROM employees) t
WHERE r = :n LIMIT 1;

2. Find duplicate emails

SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

3. Delete duplicates, keep lowest id

DELETE FROM users u USING users v WHERE u.email = v.email AND u.id > v.id;   -- PostgreSQL

4. Top earner(s) per department

SELECT dept, name, salary FROM (
  SELECT dept, name, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) r
  FROM employees) t
WHERE r = 1;            -- r <= 3 for top 3

5. Employees earning more than their manager

SELECT e.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

6. Running total

SELECT day, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running
FROM sales;

7. Customers who never ordered (anti-join)

SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
-- or NOT EXISTS (safe with NULLs; NOT IN breaks if subquery returns a NULL)
SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

8. Departments with more than 5 employees and average salary

SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM employees GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 ORDER BY avg_sal DESC;

9. Day-over-day change / consecutive rows

SELECT day, revenue, revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS change FROM daily;
-- users who logged in 3 consecutive days: gaps-and-islands
SELECT user_id FROM (
  SELECT user_id, day, day - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day))::int AS grp
  FROM logins) t
GROUP BY user_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

10. Salary above department average

SELECT name, dept, salary FROM (
  SELECT *, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_avg FROM employees) t
WHERE salary > dept_avg;

Bonus: pivot counts per status

SELECT dept,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'ACTIVE') AS active,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'LEFT' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS left_count
FROM employees GROUP BY dept;

Remember: Top-N-per-group → window function in a subquery. "Never/not" → LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL or NOT EXISTS. Filter on aggregates → HAVING.

Trap: NOT IN (subquery) returns no rows if the subquery contains a single NULL. Prefer NOT EXISTS.

14.10 Indexes

An index is a separate sorted structure (usually a B+ tree) that maps column values to row locations so lookups take O(log n) instead of a full scan.

                          [  40  |  80  ]                     root
                 /              |              \
        [ 10 | 25 ]        [ 50 | 65 ]        [ 90 | 120 ]    internal nodes
        /   |    \          /   |   \           /   |   \
   [1..9][10..24][25..39][40..49][50..64][65..79][80..89]...  leaves (sorted keys)
      <->     <->      <->     <->     <->     <->            leaves linked: range scans

  WHERE id = 57       : root -> 50|65 -> leaf [50..64]        ~3-4 page reads
  WHERE id BETWEEN 45 AND 70 : find 45, walk right along linked leaves

Composite index: leftmost-prefix rule

INDEX idx ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at)

sorted like a phone book:  customer_id, then status, then created_at

WHERE customer_id = 7                                     uses index
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'PAID'                 uses index
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'PAID'
      AND created_at > '2026-01-01'                       uses all three
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND created_at > ...                uses customer_id part only
WHERE status = 'PAID'                                     cannot seek (no leftmost col)
WHERE customer_id > 5 AND status = 'PAID'                 range stops later columns

Remember: Equality columns first, then range, then sort column. A range condition ends the usable prefix.

When an index is NOT used

Case Example Fix
function on column WHERE LOWER(email) = ? expression index ON (LOWER(email))
leading wildcard LIKE '%son' trigram / full-text index
implicit type cast varchar_col = 123 compare same types
skipping leftmost column see above reorder or new index
low selectivity WHERE active = true (95% rows) planner prefers seq scan, correctly
OR across different columns a = 1 OR b = 2 separate indexes (bitmap OR) or UNION
arithmetic on column WHERE price * 1.1 > 100 move math to the other side
tiny table / stale stats ANALYZE
Index type Use
B-tree (default) equality, range, sort, prefix LIKE 'abc%'
Hash equality only
GIN JSONB, arrays, full-text
GiST / BRIN geometry / huge append-only time series
Covering (INCLUDE) index-only scans — no table visit
Partial (WHERE deleted = false) index only hot rows

Trap: Indexes speed reads and slow writes (every insert/update maintains each index) and cost storage. Do not index every column. Check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

Clustered vs non-clustered

Clustered: the table rows themselves are stored in index order (InnoDB primary key; one per table). Non-clustered (secondary): a separate structure pointing to rows (PostgreSQL uses heap tables, so all indexes are secondary).

14.11 Transactions, ACID and isolation

Letter Means Mechanism
Atomicity all or nothing undo log / rollback
Consistency constraints hold before and after constraints, FKs, app rules
Isolation concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work locks, MVCC
Durability committed data survives a crash write-ahead log (WAL), fsync

Anomalies

DIRTY READ           T1: UPDATE bal=0 ........ ROLLBACK
                     T2:        READ bal=0  (never committed!)

NON-REPEATABLE READ  T1: READ bal=100 ............ READ bal=50
                     T2:        UPDATE bal=50; COMMIT

PHANTOM READ         T1: COUNT(*) WHERE dept=10 -> 5 ...... COUNT -> 6
                     T2:        INSERT dept=10; COMMIT

LOST UPDATE          T1: READ stock=10 ........ WRITE stock=9
                     T2:     READ stock=10 ........ WRITE stock=9   (one sale lost)
Isolation level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom Notes
READ UNCOMMITTED possible possible possible PostgreSQL treats as READ COMMITTED
READ COMMITTED prevented possible possible PostgreSQL / Oracle / SQL Server default
REPEATABLE READ prevented prevented possible (standard) MySQL InnoDB default; PG snapshot also blocks phantoms
SERIALIZABLE prevented prevented prevented PG uses SSI: may abort with serialization failure — retry

Remember: Higher isolation = fewer anomalies, more blocking or retries. Default READ COMMITTED + explicit locking or versioning for hot rows.

MVCC in one picture

row id=1 versions:   (xmin=100, xmax=205, bal=100)   (xmin=205, xmax=inf, bal=50)
T(snapshot at 150) sees bal=100 ; T(snapshot at 210) sees bal=50
Readers never block writers, writers never block readers. Old versions -> VACUUM.

Optimistic vs pessimistic locking

@Entity
public class Product {
    @Id Long id;
    int stock;
    @Version long version;          // optimistic: UPDATE ... SET stock=?, version=v+1
}                                   //   WHERE id=? AND version=v  -> 0 rows = conflict

// pessimistic: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
@Query("select p from Product p where p.id = :id")
Optional<Product> lockById(Long id);
Optimistic Pessimistic
How version column checked at write row lock on read (FOR UPDATE)
Conflict OptimisticLockException → retry / 409 others wait
Best for low contention, long user think time high contention, short critical sections
Risk retry storms under contention deadlocks, blocked threads

Tip: For a simple counter, skip both: UPDATE product SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0 is atomic; check rows affected.

Trap: Deadlock: T1 locks A then B, T2 locks B then A. Always lock rows in a consistent order (e.g. by id) and keep transactions short.

14.12 The N+1 problem

List<Order> orders = repo.findAll();            1 query  -> 100 orders
for (o : orders) o.getCustomer().getName();     100 queries (one per lazy customer)
                                                 = N + 1 = 101 round trips
Fix How
fetch join @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.customer")
entity graph @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "customer") on the repository method
batch fetching hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50 → WHERE id IN (...) batches
DTO projection select new com.x.OrderView(o.id, c.name) from Order o join o.customer c

Trap: join fetch on a collection plus pagination makes Hibernate paginate in memory (warning HHH90003004). Page the ids first, then fetch by ids.

Remember: Turn on SQL logging (spring.jpa.show-sql or a datasource proxy) in dev; count queries per request. Default all @ManyToOne to LAZY.

14.13 SQL vs NoSQL

Need Pick
relations, joins, transactions, reporting, money SQL (PostgreSQL)
flexible document per entity, read whole aggregate document (MongoDB) or PostgreSQL JSONB
massive write throughput, time series, wide rows wide-column (Cassandra)
cache, sessions, counters, leaderboards key-value (Redis)
relationships are the query (friends of friends) graph (Neo4j)
full-text search, fuzzy, facets search engine (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch)

Tip: Interview answer: "Start with PostgreSQL unless a requirement forces otherwise — scale reads with replicas and caching, and add a specialised store for the one access pattern that needs it."

14.14 Caching with Redis

Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the default pattern: the application checks the cache, falls back to the DB on a miss, and fills the cache.

@Cacheable(value = "users", key = "#id")
public UserDto get(long id) { return repo.findById(id).map(UserDto::of).orElseThrow(); }

@CacheEvict(value = "users", key = "#id")
public void update(long id, UpdateUser u) { ... }
Strategy Write path Trade-off
cache-aside write DB, delete cache simple; brief staleness possible
write-through write cache and DB together fresh cache, slower writes
write-behind write cache, flush DB async fast, risk of loss
read-through cache library loads on miss same as cache-aside, hidden in library
Problem Fix
stampede (hot key expires, 1000 requests hit DB) lock/single-flight, early refresh, jittered TTL
penetration (keys that never exist) cache negative result briefly, Bloom filter
avalanche (many keys expire at once) random TTL jitter
stale data delete-on-write, short TTL

Remember: Delete the cache entry on write, don't update it — two concurrent writers updating the cache can leave the older value.

Redis data types worth naming: string (cache, counter with INCR), hash (object fields), list (queue), set (unique members), sorted set (leaderboard, rate limiter window), stream (event log), plus TTL and SET key val NX EX 30 for a simple distributed lock.

14.15 Message queues and Kafka basics

Queues decouple producers from consumers in time and load: the producer is fast, the consumer catches up, and a crash does not lose work.

               topic "orders" (3 partitions, replicated)
 producer --key=customerId--> P0: [m0][m3][m6][m9]  ---> consumer group "billing"
     hash(key) % 3            P1: [m1][m4][m7]      --->   C1 reads P0, P1
                              P2: [m2][m5][m8]      --->   C2 reads P2
                                   ^offset 0..n
 another group "email" reads ALL partitions independently with its own offsets
Concept Meaning
Topic named stream of records
Partition ordered, append-only log; unit of parallelism; order guaranteed within a partition
Key decides partition → same key, same order
Offset position of a record; consumer commits it
Consumer group partitions are shared among members; each partition read by one member
Replication leader + followers; acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 for durability
Retention records kept by time/size, not deleted on read (unlike RabbitMQ)
Delivery How Risk
at-most-once commit offset before processing loss
at-least-once (default) process, then commit duplicates → make consumers idempotent
exactly-once idempotent producer + transactions (Kafka to Kafka) complexity 
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "billing")
public void on(OrderPlaced e) {
    if (processed.existsById(e.eventId())) return;     // idempotent consumer
    billing.charge(e);
    processed.save(new Processed(e.eventId()));
}

Trap: Writing to the DB and then publishing to Kafka is not atomic — a crash between them loses the event. Use the transactional outbox: insert the event into an outbox table in the same DB transaction, and a relay publishes it.

Kafka RabbitMQ
log, replayable, high throughput broker queues, message deleted after ack
ordering per partition routing (exchanges, topics, fanout)
event streaming, analytics, CDC task queues, RPC, complex routing

14.16 Interview Q&A

REST and HTTP

  1. What makes an API RESTful? Resources with URLs, standard verbs, stateless requests, representations (JSON), proper status codes, cacheability.
  2. PUT vs PATCH? PUT replaces the full resource (idempotent); PATCH changes some fields.
  3. POST vs PUT? POST creates under a collection (server picks id, not idempotent); PUT creates/replaces at a known URL (idempotent).
  4. How do you make a POST safe to retry? An Idempotency-Key header stored with the response.
  5. 401 vs 403? Not authenticated vs authenticated but not permitted.
  6. 400 vs 422? Malformed request vs valid syntax that breaks business rules.
  7. Offset vs cursor pagination? Offset is simple and jumpable but slow deep and unstable under inserts; cursor uses an index seek and is stable.
  8. How do you version APIs? URL /v1 most commonly; change version only on breaking changes; deprecate with headers and timelines.
  9. What is HATEOAS? Responses include links to next actions; rarely used in practice.
  10. ETag? A version fingerprint: If-None-Match → 304 for caching; If-Match → 412 for optimistic concurrency.
  11. HTTP/2 improvements? Binary framing, multiplexing over one connection, header compression, server push (deprecated).
  12. Why HTTP/3? QUIC over UDP removes TCP head-of-line blocking and speeds up handshakes.
  13. What happens when you type a URL? DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP request, load balancer, server, DB, response, browser parse and render.

Spring Boot

  1. What does @SpringBootApplication do? @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan.
  2. How does auto-configuration work? AutoConfiguration.imports lists config classes guarded by @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty; your beans win.
  3. Explain the DispatcherServlet flow. Filters → DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → interceptors → HandlerAdapter (arg resolution, conversion, validation) → controller → message converter → response; exceptions to @ControllerAdvice.
  4. Filter vs interceptor vs AOP? Servlet-level; around handler with handler info; around any bean method.
  5. Why constructor injection? Immutable final fields, explicit required deps, testable without Spring, fails fast.
  6. Bean scopes? singleton, prototype, request, session, application.
  7. Why does @Transactional not work when I call the method from the same class? Self-invocation bypasses the proxy.
  8. Which exceptions roll back? Unchecked (RuntimeException, Error) by default; configure rollbackFor for checked.
  9. REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW? Join vs suspend-and-start-new.
  10. Global exception handling? @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods returning a consistent envelope or ProblemDetail.
  11. How do you validate input? Bean Validation annotations on DTOs, @Valid on @RequestBody, @Validated for params, custom ConstraintValidator.
  12. @Component vs @Bean? Class-level scanning vs method in a @Configuration (for third-party classes or custom construction).
  13. Spring profiles? application-{profile}.yml and @Profile for environment-specific beans and config.
  14. Actuator? Health, metrics (Micrometer), info, env endpoints for operations.

Security

  1. Session vs JWT? Stateful, easy revoke, CSRF risk vs stateless, scalable, hard to revoke.
  2. What is in a JWT and how is it verified? Header, payload, signature; verify signature with the issuer key, then exp, iss, aud.
  3. OAuth2 Authorization Code with PKCE? Browser gets a one-time code via redirect, exchanges it with the code verifier for tokens; PKCE stops intercepted codes being used.
  4. OAuth2 vs OIDC? Authorization delegation vs identity on top (id token).
  5. How to store passwords? Never plain or fast hashes; use bcrypt/argon2 with salt (PasswordEncoder).
  6. Prevent SQL injection? Parameterised queries / JPA parameters; never concatenate input.

Databases

  1. Explain ACID. Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability.
  2. Isolation levels and anomalies? See the table in 16.11.
  3. What is MVCC? Multiple row versions so readers see a snapshot without blocking writers.
  4. How does a B-tree index work? Balanced sorted tree, log-n lookups, linked leaves for ranges.
  5. Composite index order? Leftmost prefix; equality columns first, then range.
  6. Why is my index not used? Functions on columns, leading wildcard, type mismatch, low selectivity, missing leftmost column.
  7. N+1 problem? One query for parents plus one per child; fix with fetch join, entity graph, batch size or projection.
  8. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking? @Version check at write vs SELECT FOR UPDATE.
  9. WHERE vs HAVING? Row filter before grouping vs group filter after aggregation.
  10. RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER? Gaps after ties; no gaps; always unique.
  11. Normalisation? 1NF atomic values, 2NF no partial dependency on composite key, 3NF no transitive dependency; denormalise deliberately for reads.
  12. Sharding vs replication? Split data across nodes for write scale vs copy data for read scale and availability.
  13. SQL vs NoSQL? Relational + transactions vs flexible schema + specific scale patterns.
  14. Cache-aside? Read: cache, then DB and fill. Write: DB, then delete cache.
  15. Kafka ordering guarantee? Per partition only; use a key for related events.
  16. At-least-once and duplicates? Make consumers idempotent with event ids.
  17. Transactional outbox? Event row written in the same DB transaction, relayed to the broker later.

14.z Chapter cheat sheet

Trigger Pattern Template one-liner Cost
retry-safe create idempotency key store key → response 1 lookup
deep pages slow keyset pagination WHERE id > :cursor ORDER BY id LIMIT n O(log n)
tx ignored proxy trap call from another bean, public method —
checked exception no rollback rollback rule rollbackFor = Exception.class —
invalid body Bean Validation @Valid @RequestBody + @RestControllerAdvice —
stateless auth JWT resource server oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt()) verify sig
Nth highest window DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY sal DESC) = n O(n log n)
top per group window RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY g ...) in subquery —
"never did X" anti-join NOT EXISTS (...) —
slow WHERE index leftmost prefix; no function on column O(log n)
lost update locking @Version or FOR UPDATE —
101 queries N+1 join fetch / @EntityGraph 1 query
hot reads cache-aside @Cacheable + @CacheEvict O(1)
DB + event outbox event row in same tx —
ordered events Kafka key same key → same partition —

Never forget

  • Nouns in URLs, verbs in methods; POST is the only non-idempotent write.
  • 401 = who are you; 403 = not allowed; 409 = conflict; 422 = rule broken.
  • Cursor pagination for feeds; offset only when users jump to page numbers.
  • Filter → DispatcherServlet → interceptor → controller → advice on error.
  • Constructor injection with final fields.
  • @Transactional: public, called from another bean, unchecked exceptions roll back.
  • JWT is signed, not encrypted; validate signature, exp, iss, aud.
  • SQL logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
  • Top-N per group = window function in a subquery.
  • NOT EXISTS beats NOT IN when NULLs are possible.
  • Composite index: equality first, range last; a range ends the prefix.
  • PostgreSQL default isolation is READ COMMITTED; MySQL is REPEATABLE READ.
  • N+1 → fetch join or entity graph; all @ManyToOne LAZY.
  • Cache-aside: delete on write, TTL with jitter.
  • At-least-once delivery means idempotent consumers; DB + event means outbox.

15. System Design and Low-Level Design for Full-Stack

System design rounds are judged on structure, not on the "right" answer: do you clarify, estimate, draw a sensible baseline, then go deep on the hard part and name the trade-offs. Low-level design (LLD) rounds are judged on clean classes, clear responsibilities and correct concurrency. This chapter gives you a framework for both, the building blocks, six worked designs, five LLD problems and the patterns interviewers ask about most.

15.1 The 45-minute framework

Say this at the start: "Let me clarify requirements first, then do rough numbers, define the API and data model, draw the high-level design, and then go deep on the hardest part."

Step Ask / produce
Functional requirements 3–5 core features; explicitly drop the rest ("out of scope: analytics, admin")
Non-functional users (DAU), read/write ratio, latency target, availability vs consistency, durability, geography
Estimates QPS (avg and peak), storage per year, bandwidth, cache size
API 3–5 endpoints with method, path, request, response
Data model tables/collections, keys, indexes, which store and why
High-level client → LB → stateless services → cache → DB, queue, object store, CDN
Deep dive the part that is actually hard: ID generation, fan-out, ordering, hot keys, consistency
Trade-offs what fails first at 10x, single points of failure, what you would monitor

Remember: Requirements → numbers → API → data → boxes → deep dive → trade-offs. Never draw boxes before you have numbers.

Tip: Drive the conversation. Every few minutes ask "Would you like me to go deeper here, or move on?"

15.2 Back-of-envelope numbers

Quantity Value
Seconds per day 86,400 ≈ 10^5
1 M requests/day ≈ 12 QPS (peak ×2–5)
100 M requests/day ≈ 1,200 QPS
L1 cache / main memory reference 1 ns / 100 ns
SSD random read ~100 µs
Read 1 MB sequentially from memory / SSD ~10 µs / ~1 ms
Round trip same data centre ~0.5 ms
Round trip cross-continent ~150 ms
Redis GET < 1 ms
Simple indexed PostgreSQL query 1–5 ms
One PostgreSQL primary ~5–10 K writes/s, 10s of K reads/s
One Redis node ~100 K ops/s
One Kafka broker ~100s of MB/s
char / int / long / UUID 1–2 B / 4 B / 8 B / 16 B 
estimate template (URL shortener):
  writes: 100 M new URLs / month  -> 100M / (30 * 10^5) ~ 40 writes/s, peak ~200
  reads : 100:1 ratio             -> 4,000 reads/s, peak ~20,000
  storage: 500 B per row * 100M * 12 * 5 years = 3 TB
  cache : 20% of daily reads hot  -> 0.2 * 350M * 500 B ~ 35 GB  (fits in Redis)

Remember: 1 day ≈ 10^5 s. Divide daily count by 10^5 for QPS, multiply by 5 for peak.

15.3 Building blocks

Load balancer

Spreads requests across stateless instances and removes unhealthy ones.

Layer Sees Example
L4 IP + port (TCP/UDP) AWS NLB — fast, no content routing
L7 HTTP path, headers, cookies Nginx, AWS ALB, Spring Cloud Gateway — path routing, TLS termination

Algorithms: round robin, weighted, least connections, IP hash / consistent hash (stickiness).

CDN

Edge servers near users cache static assets (JS, CSS, images, video) and even API responses with Cache-Control. Pull CDN fetches from origin on the first miss; push CDN is uploaded ahead.

Cache layers

browser cache -> CDN edge -> API gateway cache -> app in-memory (Caffeine) -> Redis -> DB buffer
   fastest, least shared  ----------------------------------------------->  slowest, most shared

Database scaling

Technique Solves Cost
Vertical scaling everything, briefly ceiling, single point of failure
Read replicas read throughput, HA replication lag → read-your-writes issues
Partitioning (one DB) huge tables (by date) query must include partition key
Sharding write throughput, size cross-shard joins/transactions, resharding
Denormalisation read latency write amplification, consistency

Trap: After a user writes, reading from a lagging replica shows old data. Route that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds, or read by version.

Consistent hashing

With hash(key) % N, adding one server remaps almost every key. Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring; a key belongs to the next server clockwise, so adding a server moves only ~1/N of keys.

                    0 / 2^32
                 .--- A ---.
             k1 *           * k2          k1 -> B (next clockwise)
           /                   \          k2 -> B? no: k2 -> C
          D                     B         add server E between D and A:
           \                   /            only keys between D and E move to E
             k4 *           * k3
                 '--- C ---'
   virtual nodes: each server placed at ~100-200 points -> even spread

Remember: Ring + clockwise owner + virtual nodes. Used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, CDN and cache clusters.

CAP and PACELC

During a network Partition, a distributed store chooses Consistency (refuse some requests) or Availability (answer with possibly stale data). PACELC adds: Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency.

Choose Example Fits
CP single-primary PostgreSQL, ZooKeeper, etcd payments, inventory, bookings
AP Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), DNS feeds, likes, carts, presence

Rate limiter algorithms

TOKEN BUCKET (capacity 4, refill 1/s)        allows bursts up to capacity
  t=0  [● ● ● ●]  4 requests -> all pass  [ ]
  t=1  [●]        1 refill   -> 1 passes
  t=1  [ ]        next request -> 429

LEAKY BUCKET (queue, drains at fixed rate)   smooths output
  in: ||||| bursts --> [queue ▒▒▒▒] --> out: | | | | | steady

FIXED WINDOW (limit 3/min)                   simple, boundary burst problem
  |-- 12:00 --|-- 12:01 --|
          x x x x x x        6 requests in 2 s across the boundary all pass

SLIDING WINDOW LOG / COUNTER                 accurate
  count = curr + prev * (overlap fraction) = 2 + 3 * 0.6 = 3.8  -> limit 4 -> allow
Algorithm Memory Bursts Accuracy
Token bucket 2 numbers / key allowed to capacity good — most used (AWS, Stripe)
Leaky bucket queue smoothed good
Fixed window counter 1 counter 2x at edges rough
Sliding window log every timestamp none exact, memory heavy
Sliding window counter 2 counters small approximate, cheap

15.4 Design: URL shortener

Requirements. Shorten a long URL, redirect a short code, optional custom alias and expiry. 100 M new URLs per month, 100:1 read-heavy, redirect p99 < 50 ms.

API.

POST /api/urls        { longUrl, alias?, expiresAt? }  -> 201 { code, shortUrl }
GET  /{code}          -> 301/302 Location: longUrl     (302 if you need click analytics)

Data model. urls(code PK varchar(8), long_url text, user_id, created_at, expires_at).

Code generation. Base62 (a–z, A–Z, 0–9) with 7 characters = 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes.

Approach How Trade-off
hash + truncate MD5(url) first 7 chars collisions → check and retry
counter + base62 global ID → base62 unique, but predictable; counter is a hotspot
ID ranges each server leases a block of 1,000 IDs from DB/ZooKeeper unique, fast, no coordination per request
Snowflake ID timestamp + machine + sequence, 64-bit sortable, distributed 
static String base62(long n) {
    String a = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";
    var sb = new StringBuilder();
    do { sb.append(a.charAt((int) (n % 62))); n /= 62; } while (n > 0);
    return sb.reverse().toString();
}

Deep dive. Cache hot codes in Redis (LRU, 35 GB fits); the redirect path is one cache read. 301 is cached by browsers (less load, no analytics); 302 hits you every time. Expired rows are lazily rejected on read and cleaned by a batch job.

Tip: Abuse controls: rate limit creates per user/IP, block malicious domains with a safe-browsing check.

15.5 Design: rate limiter

Requirements. Limit each API key to N requests per window across many gateway instances, add < 2 ms latency, return 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining.

Token bucket in Redis must be atomic across instances — run it as a Lua script (or INCR + EXPIRE for a fixed window):

-- KEYS[1]=bucket  ARGV: capacity, refillPerSec, nowMs
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or capacity
local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * refill)
if tokens < 1 then return 0 end
redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens - 1, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], 60000)
return 1

Same algorithm in Java for a single instance:

final class TokenBucket {
    private final long capacity; private final double refillPerMs;
    private double tokens; private long last;
    TokenBucket(long capacity, double perSecond) {
        this.capacity = capacity; this.refillPerMs = perSecond / 1000.0;
        this.tokens = capacity; this.last = System.currentTimeMillis();
    }
    synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - last) * refillPerMs);   // refill lazily
        last = now;
        if (tokens < 1) return false;
        tokens -= 1;
        return true;
    }
}

Trap: Read-then-write in two Redis calls races between instances. Atomic Lua or INCR is required. Decide fail-open (allow if Redis is down) vs fail-closed explicitly.

15.6 Design: chat application

Requirements. 1:1 and group chat, online presence, delivery/read receipts, history, offline push. 50 M DAU, 40 messages/user/day → 2 B messages/day ≈ 23 K msg/s.

Why WebSockets. HTTP polling wastes requests; long polling holds requests; WebSocket is one persistent full-duplex TCP connection per client — the server pushes instantly. SSE is server→client only.

Deep dive.

  • Message table partitioned by conversation_id, clustered by seq → one partition read returns history in order.
  • Ordering: a per-conversation sequence number assigned by the server; clients sort by it.
  • Idempotency: client-generated clientMsgId so retries do not duplicate.
  • Presence: heartbeat every 30 s refreshes presence:user with 60 s TTL; publish changes only to friends who are online.
  • Offline: if no connection is found, enqueue a push notification; on reconnect the client syncs from its last seen seq.
  • Group fan-out: small groups fan out on write; very large channels are pulled.

Remember: WebSocket servers are stateful → keep a user→server registry and use a pub/sub bus between servers.

15.7 Design: news feed

Requirements. Post, follow, see a home feed of followed users' posts ranked by time. 300 M DAU, feed reads ≫ posts.

Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull)
On post write post id into every follower's feed cache write once
On read read one precomputed list — fast query all followees, merge — slow
Problem celebrities with 50 M followers slow reads for users following many
Hybrid push for normal users pull celebrities' posts at read time and merge

Tip: Store only post ids in feeds, hydrate content from a post cache. Page with a cursor (last post id/timestamp), never with offset.

15.8 Design: notification system

Requirements. Send email, SMS, push and in-app notifications triggered by services; user preferences and quiet hours; retries; no duplicates; 10 M notifications/day with spikes.

Key points: one queue per channel so a slow SMS vendor does not block email; retries with exponential backoff and jitter; a dead-letter queue for poison messages; dedupe on (eventId, userId, channel); rate limits per user to avoid spam; templates rendered with locale; tracking (sent, delivered, opened).

Trap: Sending inside the business transaction couples you to the vendor's latency. Publish an event (outbox) and let workers send asynchronously.

15.9 Design: file upload and storage

Requirements. Upload files up to 5 GB, download quickly worldwide, virus scan, thumbnails for images.

Decision Choice Why
Data path client → object store directly via presigned URL app servers don't proxy gigabytes
Large files multipart / chunked, resumable retry one 8 MB part, not 5 GB
Metadata PostgreSQL files(id, owner, key, size, status, checksum) queryable
Download CDN with signed URLs fast, private
Dedup content hash (SHA-256) store identical files once
Processing event → queue → workers async, scalable

Remember: Bytes go to object storage, metadata goes to the database, nothing large flows through your API.

15.10 SOLID

Principle One line Smell when broken
Single responsibility a class has one reason to change InvoiceService that also formats PDFs and sends email
Open/closed extend by adding code, not editing it switch (type) growing in many places
Liskov substitution a subtype works anywhere its parent does Square extends Rectangle breaking setWidth
Interface segregation small focused interfaces clients implementing methods with throw new UnsupportedOperationException()
Dependency inversion depend on abstractions, inject them new MySqlRepo() inside a service 
// O + D: add a new payment method without touching checkout
interface PaymentMethod { Receipt pay(Money amount); }
record Card(String token) implements PaymentMethod { public Receipt pay(Money m) { /* ... */ return null; } }
record Upi(String vpa)   implements PaymentMethod { public Receipt pay(Money m) { /* ... */ return null; } }

final class Checkout {
    Receipt complete(Cart cart, PaymentMethod pm) { return pm.pay(cart.total()); }
}

15.11 The six most-asked design patterns

Singleton — one instance, global access.

public enum Config { INSTANCE; public String get(String k) { return System.getenv(k); } }

// or lazy holder (thread-safe without synchronisation)
final class Registry {
    private Registry() {}
    private static class Holder { static final Registry I = new Registry(); }
    static Registry get() { return Holder.I; }
}

Factory — callers ask for an interface; the factory decides the class.

static Notifier notifier(String channel) {
    return switch (channel) {
        case "email" -> new EmailNotifier();
        case "sms"   -> new SmsNotifier();
        default      -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(channel);
    };
}

Builder — readable construction with many optional fields, immutable result.

final class Pizza {
    private final String size; private final boolean cheese, olives;
    private Pizza(Builder b) { size = b.size; cheese = b.cheese; olives = b.olives; }
    static Builder builder(String size) { return new Builder(size); }
    static final class Builder {
        private final String size; private boolean cheese, olives;
        Builder(String size) { this.size = size; }
        Builder cheese() { cheese = true; return this; }
        Builder olives() { olives = true; return this; }
        Pizza build() { return new Pizza(this); }
    }
}
// Pizza p = Pizza.builder("L").cheese().build();

Strategy — a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface.

interface PricingStrategy { long price(long base); }
PricingStrategy regular = b -> b;
PricingStrategy weekend = b -> b * 12 / 10;
PricingStrategy member  = b -> b * 9 / 10;
long total = weekend.price(20000);

Observer — subscribers are notified when a subject changes.

final class EventBus<T> {
    private final List<Consumer<T>> subs = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
    void subscribe(Consumer<T> s) { subs.add(s); }
    void publish(T event) { subs.forEach(s -> s.accept(event)); }
}

Decorator — wrap an object to add behaviour while keeping the same interface.

interface DataSource { String read(); }
record FileSource(String path) implements DataSource { public String read() { return "data"; } }
record Decompressing(DataSource inner) implements DataSource {
    public String read() { return "unzip(" + inner.read() + ")"; }
}
record Logging(DataSource inner) implements DataSource {
    public String read() { System.out.println("read"); return inner.read(); }
}
// new Logging(new Decompressing(new FileSource("a.gz"))).read();
Pattern In the JDK / Spring
Singleton Spring singleton beans, Runtime.getRuntime()
Factory List.of, BeanFactory, Executors.newFixedThreadPool
Builder StringBuilder, HttpRequest.newBuilder(), ResponseEntity.ok().body()
Strategy Comparator, Spring PasswordEncoder
Observer ApplicationEventPublisher + @EventListener
Decorator BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream()), Spring AOP proxies

Trap: Double-checked locking without volatile is broken. Use an enum or the holder idiom.

15.12 LLD: Parking lot

Say: "Lot has floors, floors have spots of sizes; a vehicle gets the first free spot that fits; a ticket records entry time; a pricing strategy computes the fee on exit."

enum VehicleType { BIKE, CAR, TRUCK }
enum SpotSize { SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE }
record Vehicle(String plate, VehicleType type) {}
record Ticket(String id, Vehicle vehicle, Spot spot, Instant entry) {}

final class Spot {
    final String id; final SpotSize size; private Vehicle occupant;
    Spot(String id, SpotSize size) { this.id = id; this.size = size; }
    boolean fits(VehicleType t) { return occupant == null && size.ordinal() >= t.ordinal(); }
    void park(Vehicle v) { occupant = v; }
    void free() { occupant = null; }
}

final class ParkingLot {
    private final List<Spot> spots;
    private final Map<String, Ticket> active = new HashMap<>();
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;
    ParkingLot(List<Spot> spots, PricingStrategy pricing) { this.spots = spots; this.pricing = pricing; }

    synchronized Ticket park(Vehicle v) {                       // one lock: no double booking
        Spot s = spots.stream().filter(x -> x.fits(v.type())).findFirst()
                      .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("Lot full"));
        s.park(v);
        var t = new Ticket(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), v, s, Instant.now());
        active.put(t.id(), t);
        return t;
    }
    synchronized long unpark(String ticketId) {
        Ticket t = active.remove(ticketId);
        if (t == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown ticket");
        t.spot().free();
        return pricing.fee(t, Instant.now());
    }
}
interface PricingStrategy { long fee(Ticket t, Instant exit); }

Tip: Extensions to mention: per-size free-spot queues for O(1) allocation, display boards via Observer, multiple entry gates (finer-grained locks per floor).

15.13 LLD: LRU cache

Say: "HashMap for O(1) lookup plus a doubly linked list for O(1) recency order; head = most recent, tail = least recent."

map: {1 -> n1, 2 -> n2, 3 -> n3}
head <-> [3] <-> [1] <-> [2] <-> tail        get(2): move n2 to front
head <-> [2] <-> [3] <-> [1] <-> tail        put(4) at capacity 3: evict tail.prev = [1]
head <-> [4] <-> [2] <-> [3] <-> tail
final class LRUCache {
    private final class Node { int key, val; Node prev, next; Node(int k, int v) { key = k; val = v; } }
    private final int cap;
    private final Map<Integer, Node> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node head = new Node(0, 0), tail = new Node(0, 0);   // sentinels

    LRUCache(int cap) { this.cap = cap; head.next = tail; tail.prev = head; }

    public int get(int key) {
        Node n = map.get(key);
        if (n == null) return -1;
        remove(n); addFront(n);
        return n.val;
    }
    public void put(int key, int val) {
        Node n = map.get(key);
        if (n != null) { n.val = val; remove(n); addFront(n); return; }
        if (map.size() == cap) { Node lru = tail.prev; remove(lru); map.remove(lru.key); }
        n = new Node(key, val); addFront(n); map.put(key, n);
    }
    private void remove(Node n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; }
    private void addFront(Node n) { n.next = head.next; n.prev = head; head.next.prev = n; head.next = n; }
}

Remember: Store the key inside the node — you need it to delete from the map on eviction. Java shortcut: LinkedHashMap(cap, 0.75f, true) + override removeEldestEntry.

Tip: Thread-safe follow-up: wrap methods in a ReentrantLock, or shard into N segments each with its own lock.

15.14 LLD: Elevator

Say: "Each elevator is a state machine; a dispatcher assigns hall calls to the best elevator; each elevator serves requests in its current direction first (SCAN / LOOK)."

enum Direction { UP, DOWN, IDLE }

final class Elevator {
    final int id; int floor = 0; Direction dir = Direction.IDLE;
    private final TreeSet<Integer> up = new TreeSet<>(), down = new TreeSet<>();
    Elevator(int id) { this.id = id; }

    void addStop(int f) { if (f > floor) up.add(f); else if (f < floor) down.add(f); }

    void step() {                                               // called on each tick
        if (dir != Direction.DOWN && !up.isEmpty()) { dir = Direction.UP; floor = up.pollFirst(); }
        else if (!down.isEmpty()) { dir = Direction.DOWN; floor = down.pollLast(); }
        else if (!up.isEmpty()) { dir = Direction.UP; floor = up.pollFirst(); }
        else dir = Direction.IDLE;
    }
    int cost(int f) { return Math.abs(floor - f) + (dir == Direction.IDLE ? 0 : 2); }
}

final class Dispatcher {
    private final List<Elevator> cars;
    Dispatcher(List<Elevator> cars) { this.cars = cars; }
    Elevator call(int floor) {                                  // strategy: nearest car
        Elevator best = cars.stream().min(Comparator.comparingInt(e -> e.cost(floor))).orElseThrow();
        best.addStop(floor);
        return best;
    }
}

Tip: Make the dispatch rule a Strategy (nearest car, least loaded, zoning) — that is the extension the interviewer is waiting for.

15.15 LLD: Splitwise

Say: "Users, groups and expenses; an expense has a payer and a split strategy (equal, exact, percent); a balance sheet tracks net amounts; settle-up minimises transactions greedily."

record User(String id) {}
record Share(User user, long amount) {}
record Transfer(String from, String to, long amount) {}

final class EqualSplit {
    static List<Share> of(long amount, List<User> users) {
        long each = amount / users.size(), rem = amount % users.size();
        var res = new ArrayList<Share>();
        for (int i = 0; i < users.size(); i++)                   // first 'rem' users pay 1 more paisa
            res.add(new Share(users.get(i), each + (i < rem ? 1 : 0)));
        return res;
    }
}

final class BalanceSheet {
    private final Map<String, Long> net = new HashMap<>();      // + is owed, - owes
    void add(User payer, long amount, List<Share> shares) {
        net.merge(payer.id(), amount, Long::sum);
        for (Share s : shares) net.merge(s.user().id(), -s.amount(), Long::sum);
    }
    List<Transfer> settle() {                                    // greedy: largest debtor -> largest creditor
        var cred = new PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>>((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.getValue(), a.getValue()));
        var debt = new PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>>((a, b) -> Long.compare(a.getValue(), b.getValue()));
        net.forEach((k, v) -> { if (v > 0) cred.add(Map.entry(k, v)); else if (v < 0) debt.add(Map.entry(k, v)); });
        var res = new ArrayList<Transfer>();
        while (!cred.isEmpty() && !debt.isEmpty()) {
            var c = cred.poll(); var d = debt.poll();
            long x = Math.min(c.getValue(), -d.getValue());
            res.add(new Transfer(d.getKey(), c.getKey(), x));
            if (c.getValue() - x > 0) cred.add(Map.entry(c.getKey(), c.getValue() - x));
            if (d.getValue() + x < 0) debt.add(Map.entry(d.getKey(), d.getValue() + x));
        }
        return res;
    }
}
A paid 300 for A,B,C (equal 100 each):  net A=+200, B=-100, C=-100
B paid 60 for B,C (30 each):            net B=-100+60-30=-70, C=-100-30=-130
settle: C -> A 130, B -> A 70           (2 transfers)

Trap: Never use double for money. Store integer paise/cents (or BigDecimal) and distribute the remainder explicitly.

15.16 LLD: BookMyShow seat locking

The hard part is concurrency: two users must never pay for the same seat. Say: "Seats are temporarily locked for ~10 minutes while the user pays; the lock is atomic and expires on its own; the booking is confirmed only if the lock is still held."

-- DB-level atomic lock: succeeds only for seats still available or expired
UPDATE show_seat
SET status = 'LOCKED', locked_by = :user, locked_until = now() + interval '10 minutes'
WHERE show_id = :show AND seat_id IN (:seats)
  AND (status = 'AVAILABLE' OR (status = 'LOCKED' AND locked_until < now()));
-- rows updated must equal number of seats, otherwise roll back the transaction
@Transactional
public Booking lock(long showId, List<Long> seats, String user) {
    int n = seatRepo.lockSeats(showId, seats, user);            // the UPDATE above
    if (n != seats.size()) throw new SeatUnavailableException(); // rollback releases partial locks
    return bookingRepo.save(Booking.pending(showId, seats, user));
}

@Transactional
public void confirm(long bookingId, String paymentId) {
    Booking b = bookingRepo.findById(bookingId).orElseThrow();
    int n = seatRepo.markBooked(b.showId(), b.seats(), b.user()); // WHERE locked_by = user AND locked_until > now()
    if (n != b.seats().size()) { payments.refund(paymentId); throw new LockExpiredException(); }
    b.confirm(paymentId);
}
Option How Note
Conditional UPDATE (above) atomic row update with predicate simplest, strongly consistent
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE pessimistic row locks lock seats in id order to avoid deadlocks
@Version optimistic many 409s on hot shows
Redis SET seat:show:id user NX EX 600 distributed lock with TTL fast; DB still the source of truth
Unique constraint (show_id, seat_id) on bookings last line of defence

Remember: Lock with TTL → pay → confirm only if the lock is still yours → otherwise refund. Lock multiple seats all-or-nothing.

15.17 Extra building blocks interviewers probe

Unique IDs at scale (Snowflake)

 64-bit id
 +---+-------------------------------+------------+--------------+
 | 0 | 41 bits: ms since custom epoch| 10 bits:   | 12 bits:     |
 |   | (~69 years)                   | machine id | sequence/ms  |
 +---+-------------------------------+------------+--------------+
 -> roughly time-sortable, 4,096 ids per ms per machine, no coordination per id
 risk: clock moving backwards -> refuse to issue until clock catches up
Option Sortable Coordination Size
DB auto-increment yes single DB is a bottleneck 8 B
UUID v4 no (random, bad for B-tree locality) none 16 B
UUID v7 yes (time prefix) none 16 B
Snowflake yes machine id assignment 8 B
ID ranges per block one DB call per block 8 B

Idempotency, retries and timeouts

Every remote call needs a timeout, a bounded retry with exponential backoff plus jitter, and an idempotent receiver. Add a circuit breaker (Resilience4j) so a dead dependency fails fast instead of exhausting threads.

Observability

Signal Tool Answers
Metrics Micrometer → Prometheus → Grafana is it healthy? RED: rate, errors, duration
Logs structured JSON → Loki / ELK what happened for this request?
Traces OpenTelemetry → Tempo / Jaeger where did the 2 seconds go across services?
Alerts SLO burn rate should someone wake up?

Microservices vs modular monolith

Modular monolith Microservices
Deploy one unit independent per service
Data one DB, module-owned schemas database per service
Consistency local transactions sagas, outbox, eventual consistency
Ops cost low high: discovery, tracing, gateways, many pipelines
Choose when small team, unclear boundaries many teams, different scaling needs

Tip: A saga replaces a distributed transaction with a sequence of local transactions plus compensating actions (reserve stock → charge card → if charge fails, release stock). Orchestrated (a coordinator) or choreographed (events).

15.18 Interview Q&A

  1. How do you start a system design interview? Clarify functional and non-functional requirements, agree on scope, then estimate.
  2. How do you scale a read-heavy system? Cache (CDN, Redis), read replicas, denormalised read models, pagination.
  3. How do you scale a write-heavy system? Batch and queue writes, shard by a high-cardinality key, append-only stores (Kafka, Cassandra).
  4. Vertical vs horizontal scaling? Bigger machine vs more machines; horizontal needs stateless services.
  5. Why stateless services? Any instance can serve any request, so you can add, remove and replace instances freely.
  6. How do you choose a shard key? High cardinality, evenly distributed, present in most queries; avoid monotonic keys (hot last shard) and celebrity keys.
  7. What is replication lag and how do you handle it? Replicas trail the primary; read-your-writes from the primary or wait for a version.
  8. Explain consistent hashing. Keys and nodes on a ring, key owned by next node clockwise, virtual nodes for balance; adding a node moves ~1/N keys.
  9. Explain CAP. Under a partition, choose consistency or availability; without one, trade latency vs consistency (PACELC).
  10. Strong vs eventual consistency? Every read sees the latest write vs replicas converge over time.
  11. Which rate limiting algorithm would you pick? Token bucket: cheap, allows controlled bursts, atomic in Redis.
  12. Where does the rate limiter live? API gateway or middleware, with shared state in Redis; also per-service for protection.
  13. How do you generate short codes? Pre-allocated ID ranges encoded in base62, or hash with collision check.
  14. 301 or 302 for a shortener? 301 is cached by browsers (less load); 302 lets you count every click.
  15. WebSocket vs SSE vs long polling? Full duplex vs server-push only over HTTP vs repeated held requests; chat needs WebSocket, live dashboards can use SSE.
  16. How do you scale WebSocket servers? L4 load balancing, connection registry in Redis, pub/sub between servers, graceful reconnect with last-seen sequence.
  17. How do you guarantee message ordering in chat? Server-assigned per-conversation sequence numbers; Kafka key = conversation id.
  18. Push vs pull feed? Push precomputes per follower (fast reads, expensive for celebrities); pull merges at read time; hybrid wins.
  19. How do you make notifications reliable? Outbox, per-channel queues, retries with backoff, dead-letter queue, dedupe keys, delivery log.
  20. How do you upload a 5 GB file? Presigned multipart upload straight to object storage, resumable parts, completion callback, async processing.
  21. What is a CDN and what do you put on it? Edge cache close to users: static assets, images, video, cacheable API responses.
  22. When do you add a message queue? To absorb spikes, decouple slow work, fan out events, and retry safely.
  23. How do you avoid a cache stampede? Single-flight lock per key, stale-while-revalidate, jittered TTLs.
  24. How do you design for failure? Redundancy across zones, timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, graceful degradation.
  25. What is a saga? Local transactions with compensations instead of a distributed two-phase commit.
  26. Explain SOLID briefly. One reason to change; extend without editing; subtypes substitutable; small interfaces; depend on abstractions.
  27. Strategy vs State pattern? Strategy is chosen by the client to vary an algorithm; State changes itself as the object's state changes.
  28. Decorator vs inheritance? Decorator composes behaviour at runtime and stacks; inheritance fixes it at compile time and explodes into subclasses.
  29. How do you make a singleton thread-safe? Enum or the static holder idiom; double-checked locking needs volatile.
  30. How do you prevent double booking? Atomic conditional update or row lock, TTL-based hold, confirm only while the hold is owned, unique constraint as backstop.
  31. How would you make the LRU cache thread-safe? A lock around get/put, or lock striping by key hash; ConcurrentHashMap alone is not enough because the list must change too.
  32. How do you minimise transactions in Splitwise? Compute net balances, then greedily match the largest debtor with the largest creditor.

Trigger Pattern Template one-liner Cost
any HLD question 45-min framework reqs → estimates → API → data → boxes → deep dive —

Never forget

  • Clarify requirements and non-goals before drawing anything.
  • 1 day ≈ 10^5 s; 1 M/day ≈ 12 QPS.
  • Stateless services behind a load balancer; state lives in DB, cache, object store.
  • Replicas scale reads and add lag; sharding scales writes and breaks joins.
  • Consistent hashing moves only ~1/N keys when a node joins.
  • CP for money and bookings, AP for feeds and likes.
  • Token bucket is the default rate limiter; make it atomic.
  • 301 is cached (no analytics), 302 is not.
  • WebSocket servers are stateful — registry plus pub/sub.
  • Feeds: hybrid fan-out, ids only, cursor paging.
  • Notifications: per-channel queues, retries with backoff, dead-letter queue, dedupe.
  • Files: presigned upload straight to object storage.
  • LRU = map + doubly linked list with sentinels; keep the key in the node.
  • Money in integer minor units, never double.
  • Seat booking = atomic lock with TTL, confirm only if still owned.

16.2 Core templates

Shared definitions:

class ListNode { int val; ListNode next; ListNode(int v) { val = v; } }
class TreeNode { int val; TreeNode left, right; TreeNode(int v) { val = v; } }

Binary search (lower bound)

// first index with a[i] >= target (returns a.length if none)
int lowerBound(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length;              // half-open [lo, hi)
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;       // no overflow
        if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid;
    }
    return lo;
}
a = [1 3 3 5 8], target 3
lo=0 hi=5 mid=2 a[2]=3 >= 3 -> hi=2
lo=0 hi=2 mid=1 a[1]=3 >= 3 -> hi=1
lo=0 hi=1 mid=0 a[0]=1 <  3 -> lo=1      answer 1

Binary search on the answer

int minFeasible(int lo, int hi) {           // smallest x in [lo, hi] with ok(x) true
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (ok(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}

Sliding window (variable size)

int longestUniqueSubstring(String s) {
    int[] cnt = new int[128];
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < s.length(); r++) {
        cnt[s.charAt(r)]++;                         // expand
        while (cnt[s.charAt(r)] > 1) cnt[s.charAt(l++)]--;   // shrink until valid
        best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);           // record
    }
    return best;
}
s = a b c a b      window [l..r]
r=0 [a]        best 1
r=2 [a b c]    best 3
r=3 [a b c a]  dup a -> l=1 -> [b c a]  best 3

Two pointers (sorted pair sum)

int[] twoSumSorted(int[] a, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        int sum = a[l] + a[r];
        if (sum == target) return new int[]{l, r};
        if (sum < target) l++; else r--;
    }
    return new int[]{-1, -1};
}

Fast and slow pointers

boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
ListNode middle(ListNode head) {            // second middle for even length
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; }
    return slow;
}

Reverse a linked list

ListNode reverse(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null, cur = head;
    while (cur != null) {
        ListNode next = cur.next;           // save
        cur.next = prev;                    // flip
        prev = cur; cur = next;             // advance
    }
    return prev;
}
null <- 1    2 -> 3 -> null     prev=1 cur=2
null <- 1 <- 2    3 -> null     prev=2 cur=3
null <- 1 <- 2 <- 3             prev=3 cur=null  return prev

BFS (shortest steps, by level)

int bfs(Map<Integer, List<Integer>> g, int start, int goal) {
    Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
    q.offer(start); seen.add(start);                // mark when ENQUEUED
    for (int steps = 0; !q.isEmpty(); steps++) {
        for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
            int u = q.poll();
            if (u == goal) return steps;
            for (int v : g.getOrDefault(u, List.of()))
                if (seen.add(v)) q.offer(v);
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

DFS on a grid

int numIslands(char[][] grid) {
    int res = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < grid.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < grid[0].length; c++)
            if (grid[r][c] == '1') { res++; sink(grid, r, c); }
    return res;
}
void sink(char[][] g, int r, int c) {
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= g.length || c >= g[0].length || g[r][c] != '1') return;
    g[r][c] = '0';                                  // mark visited
    sink(g, r + 1, c); sink(g, r - 1, c); sink(g, r, c + 1); sink(g, r, c - 1);
}

Topological sort (Kahn)

int[] topo(int n, int[][] edges) {                 // edge {a, b}: a before b
    List<List<Integer>> g = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) g.add(new ArrayList<>());
    int[] indeg = new int[n];
    for (int[] e : edges) { g.get(e[0]).add(e[1]); indeg[e[1]]++; }
    Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.offer(i);
    int[] res = new int[n]; int k = 0;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int u = q.poll(); res[k++] = u;
        for (int v : g.get(u)) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.offer(v);
    }
    return k == n ? res : new int[0];              // k < n means a cycle
}

Union-find

int[] parent, rank;
void init(int n) { parent = new int[n]; rank = new int[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i; }
int find(int x) { return parent[x] == x ? x : (parent[x] = find(parent[x])); }   // path compression
boolean union(int a, int b) {
    int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
    if (ra == rb) return false;                    // already connected -> cycle edge
    if (rank[ra] < rank[rb]) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }
    parent[rb] = ra;
    if (rank[ra] == rank[rb]) rank[ra]++;
    return true;
}

Dijkstra

int[] dijkstra(List<List<int[]>> g, int src) {     // g.get(u) = list of {v, w}
    int[] dist = new int[g.size()];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    dist[src] = 0;
    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
    pq.offer(new int[]{src, 0});
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cur = pq.poll();
        int u = cur[0], d = cur[1];
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;                 // stale entry
        for (int[] e : g.get(u)) {
            int v = e[0], nd = d + e[1];
            if (nd < dist[v]) { dist[v] = nd; pq.offer(new int[]{v, nd}); }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

Backtracking (subsets, permutations, combination sum)

void subsets(int[] a, int start, List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> res) {
    res.add(new ArrayList<>(path));                // copy!
    for (int i = start; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (i > start && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;   // skip dups (array sorted)
        path.add(a[i]);                            // choose
        subsets(a, i + 1, path, res);              // explore
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);              // un-choose
    }
}
void permute(int[] a, boolean[] used, List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> res) {
    if (path.size() == a.length) { res.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); return; }
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (used[i]) continue;
        used[i] = true; path.add(a[i]);
        permute(a, used, path, res);
        used[i] = false; path.remove(path.size() - 1);
    }
}
subsets([1,2,3]) recursion tree
                    []
          /          |        \
        [1]         [2]       [3]
       /   \         |
    [1,2] [1,3]    [2,3]
      |
   [1,2,3]          8 results = 2^3

1D DP (house robber)

int rob(int[] a) {
    int prev2 = 0, prev1 = 0;                       // dp[i-2], dp[i-1]
    for (int x : a) {
        int cur = Math.max(prev1, prev2 + x);       // skip or take
        prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur;
    }
    return prev1;
}

2D DP (longest common subsequence)

int lcs(String a, String b) {
    int[][] dp = new int[a.length() + 1][b.length() + 1];   // extra row/col of zeros
    for (int i = 1; i <= a.length(); i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= b.length(); j++)
            dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)
                ? dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
                : Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
    return dp[a.length()][b.length()];
}
LCS("abc", "ac")       ""  a  c
                  ""    0  0  0
                  a     0  1  1
                  b     0  1  1
                  c     0  1  2   <- answer
diagonal +1 on match, else max(up, left)

0/1 knapsack (1D, iterate capacity backwards)

int knapsack(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
    int[] dp = new int[cap + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i < wt.length; i++)
        for (int c = cap; c >= wt[i]; c--)          // backwards: each item once
            dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], dp[c - wt[i]] + val[i]);
    return dp[cap];
}

Monotonic stack (next greater element)

int[] nextGreater(int[] a) {
    int[] res = new int[a.length];
    Arrays.fill(res, -1);
    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();      // indices, values decreasing
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        while (!stack.isEmpty() && a[stack.peek()] < a[i]) res[stack.pop()] = a[i];
        stack.push(i);
    }
    return res;
}
a = [2 1 5 3]
i=0 push 0          stack [2]
i=1 push 1          stack [2 1]
i=2 5 pops 1,0      res[1]=5 res[0]=5  stack [5]
i=3 push 3          stack [5 3]       res = [5 5 -1 -1]

Heap top-k

int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> cnt = new HashMap<>();
    for (int x : nums) cnt.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
    PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> cnt.get(a) - cnt.get(b));  // min-heap
    for (int x : cnt.keySet()) { pq.offer(x); if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll(); }
    int[] res = new int[k];
    for (int i = k - 1; i >= 0; i--) res[i] = pq.poll();
    return res;
}

Trie

class Trie {
    private final Trie[] next = new Trie[26];
    private boolean word;
    void insert(String s) {
        Trie node = this;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (node.next[c - 'a'] == null) node.next[c - 'a'] = new Trie();
            node = node.next[c - 'a'];
        }
        node.word = true;
    }
    boolean search(String s)     { Trie n = walk(s); return n != null && n.word; }
    boolean startsWith(String p) { return walk(p) != null; }
    private Trie walk(String s) {
        Trie node = this;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) if ((node = node.next[c - 'a']) == null) return null;
        return node;
    }
}

Tree DFS returning a value (diameter)

int best = 0;
int depth(TreeNode n) {
    if (n == null) return 0;
    int l = depth(n.left), r = depth(n.right);
    best = Math.max(best, l + r);                   // path through n
    return 1 + Math.max(l, r);                      // height to parent
}

Remember: Every template has the same skeleton: initialise, loop/recurse, update the answer, return. Write the skeleton first, then fill the one line that is specific to the problem.

Trap: The top template bugs: (lo + hi) / 2 overflow, marking BFS visited on poll instead of on enqueue, forgetting to copy path in backtracking, knapsack loop going forwards, Integer compared with ==, a - b comparator overflow (use Integer.compare).

Data structure operations

Structure Access Search Insert Delete Notes

Algorithms

Algorithm Time Space
Binary search O(log n) O(1)

growth for n = 1,000,000
O(1)        1
O(log n)    20
O(n)        1,000,000

rule of thumb: ~10^8 simple operations per second

Remember: Recursion depth is space. A DFS on a 10^5-node path-shaped tree uses O(n) stack — mention it, and Java may overflow around 10^4–10^5 frames.
